title: Transplant and Oncology Infectious Diseases Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent advanced self-study curriculum; not a fellowship credential)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Licensed or license-eligible physician learner with prior internal medicine/ID specialty training; ideal audience is an ID fellow/ID-trained physician.
Foundational microbiology, antimicrobial pharmacology, immunology, transplant/oncology overview and evidence appraisal.
This non-credential course cannot authorize patient care or replace supervised clinical training.
objectives: Reason across immune defects, time course, exposures, prophylaxis and organ/cancer therapy to develop prioritized differentials.
Choose and interpret diagnostic tests with awareness of host-specific limits and sampling tradeoffs.
Synthesize evidence for bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic and noninfectious syndromes in SOT, HSCT and oncology populations.
Discuss donor-derived and healthcare-associated risks using formal institutional communication pathways.
Evaluate prevention, antimicrobial stewardship, immunosuppressant interactions and team-based safety using current primary sources.
Map course concepts to the general ABIM ID exam blueprint without claiming TOID-specific exam preparation or board readiness.

units.title: Host state, risk timeline and the consultation frame
objectives: Construct a time-sensitive differential using time since transplant/cancer therapy, immune defect, prophylaxis, exposures and anatomic barriers.
Distinguish donor-derived, recipient-derived, healthcare-associated and opportunistic infection hypotheses without treating a timeline as diagnostic.
Prioritize unstable presentations and articulate a safe first-hour workup/communication plan.
topics: Net state of immunosuppression; phase after SOT/HCT; cancer/neutropenia; consult framing; escalation and team communication.
boardDomains: Immunocompromised host (5%); bacterial disease (27%); internal medicine/noninfectious (18%).
units.casePractice: Fictional timeline matrix comparing early post-operative, later opportunistic and post-chemotherapy presentations. Learner must list data needed before ranking hypotheses.
units.assessment: Submit one-page problem representation, 5-item differential and immediate safety steps; rubric: time/exposure synthesis 30%, prioritized alternatives 25%, urgent communication/safety 25%, uncertainty 20%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: Pretransplant evaluation, donor assessment and donor-derived infection
objectives: Interpret donor/recipient serology and microbiology as risk inputs, not deterministic predictions.
Identify signals needing donor-record clarification and time-critical notification/escalation through the transplant center/OPO pathway.
Explain why linked-recipient clusters and unexpected early illness should trigger a donor-derived investigation.
topics: Pretransplant risk review; CMV/EBV/toxo/TB/endemic exposures; donor history/cultures; organ-specific risk; post-transplant notification.
boardDomains: Immunocompromised host (5%); infection prevention and control (5%); viral diseases (7%).
units.casePractice: Link to AST webinar donor-recipient vignette; learners analyze only the published educational case, not actual patient data. See case rights note.
units.assessment: Create structured donor review checklist; rubric: relevant record gaps 30%, serology interpretation 25%, escalation/systems pathway 25%, avoid overcalling transmission 20%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: Diagnostic strategy and test interpretation in immunocompromised hosts
objectives: Select diagnostic sampling based on syndrome, host and pretest probability; compare culture, histopathology, antigen/serology and molecular testing.
Describe test limitations under immunosuppression and after prophylaxis/therapy.
Use imaging and tissue sampling as part of a multidisciplinary diagnosis rather than relying on isolated biomarkers.
topics: Blood cultures; tissue/sterile-site sampling; bronchoscopy/BAL; fungal biomarkers; CMV PCR vs tissue disease; radiology/pathology/microbiology integration.
boardDomains: Bacterial diseases (27%); fungal diseases (5%); viral diseases (7%); immunocompromised host (5%).
units.casePractice: PIDS educational case slide links (e.g. IFI in SOT case 1, positive PPD pre-renal evaluation). Image status/permission to reuse unverified; link only.
units.assessment: Write a diagnostic test map for a fictional syndrome; rubric: sample choice 30%, test performance/limitations 30%, differential 20%, reassessment plan 20%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: Fever and neutropenia, bacterial sepsis and antimicrobial stewardship
objectives: Use host risk, instability, prior colonization/exposure and local antibiogram to frame urgent empirical choices; do not apply a single regimen universally.
Reassess and narrow therapy when microbiology and clinical trajectory permit.
Identify source control, device evaluation, renal dosing and stewardship considerations.
topics: Neutropenia; fever; initial stabilization; resistant bacteria; bloodstream/catheter infection; source control; de-escalation and duration.
boardDomains: Bacterial diseases (27%); antimicrobial therapy (9%); infection prevention/control (5%).
units.casePractice: NCI material is patient education; IDSA febrile neutropenia guideline is archived. Pair with institution-specific current protocols, not use as current order set.
units.assessment: Critique a hypothetical antibiotic plan with no drug dose requested; rubric: urgency 25%, risk/coverage logic 25%, cultures/source control 20%, reassessment/stewardship 20%, caveats 10%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: SOT organ-specific infection syndromes and post-transplant timeline
objectives: Compare common surgical/healthcare-associated syndromes with opportunistic disease while accounting for graft anatomy and complications.
Build a differential by organ transplanted and time after transplantation.
Recognize atypical presentations and reasons for early imaging/procedural consultation.
topics: Kidney/urinary and leak; liver/biliary; lung; heart; pancreas/intestine; device and surgical-site infection; time-linked risk.
boardDomains: Immunocompromised host (5%); bacterial diseases (27%); internal medicine/noninfectious syndromes (18%).
units.casePractice: AST webinar educational case resource; do not extrapolate fictional scenario to patients. Focus on question structure, not copied donor records.
units.assessment: Build a one-page organ/time differential with red flags and team members; rubric: organ-specific anatomy 30%, timeline 25%, competing diagnoses 25%, escalation 20%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: CMV, EBV/PTLD and other viral infections in SOT/HCT
objectives: Distinguish viral replication from end-organ disease and interpret viral-load trends in clinical context.
Compare universal prophylaxis and preemptive monitoring concepts without assuming a single protocol.
Recognize resistance, toxicity and interactions requiring specialist consultation.
topics: CMV risk and prevention/treatment concepts; EBV/PTLD; BK polyomavirus; respiratory viruses; adenovirus; HHV-6; viral diagnostics.
boardDomains: Viral diseases (7%); immunocompromised host (5%); antimicrobial therapy (9%).
units.casePractice: PIDS CMV treatment/resistance, CMV SOT prevention, EBV/PTLD and BK virus slide modules; download/view from provider only, no copying/rehosting.
units.assessment: Interpret a fictional serial viral-load and symptom timeline; rubric: replication vs disease 30%, host/treatment context 25%, next tests 20%, risks/uncertainty 25%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: Invasive fungal disease, mold and endemic fungi
objectives: Differentiate major fungal syndromes in neutropenia, HSCT and SOT using host/exposure/imaging/microbiology.
Understand limitations of biomarkers and need for tissue/organism confirmation where feasible.
Compare guideline recommendations with drug interactions, organ function, toxicity and local resistance; check dates.
topics: Aspergillus; Mucorales; Candida; Pneumocystis; endemic mycoses; prophylaxis breakthrough; environmental exposure.
units.casePractice: PIDS SOT invasive fungal case and Mucorales/Candida HSCT modules are linked; their image authenticity/permissions have not been independently audited. IDSA aspergillosis guidance is 2016 and may be dated.
units.assessment: Compare two fictional fungal hypotheses with tests and therapy constraints; rubric: host risk 20%, diagnostics 30%, competing mold coverage 20%, interaction/safety 20%, source currency 10%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: HSCT, leukemia and cellular therapy infection complications
objectives: Map infection risks to conditioning, neutropenia, engraftment, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) and immune reconstitution.
Recognize common bacterial/viral/fungal and late opportunistic syndromes; distinguish infectious from noninfectious mimics.
Coordinate with hematology, transplant, pharmacy, microbiology and infection prevention.
topics: Autologous/allogeneic HCT; neutropenia; GVHD/steroids; CMV/EBV; mold; Pneumocystis; respiratory viruses; cellular therapy context.
boardDomains: Immunocompromised host (5%); bacterial diseases (27%); viruses (7%); fungi (5%).
units.casePractice: PIDS HCT GVHD infection, CMV, RSV, community respiratory virus, Candida, Mucorales, mycobacteria and PCP modules. Pediatric material is supplementary.
units.assessment: Make a phase-of-HCT risk table including mimics; rubric: phase mapping 30%, pathogen breadth 25%, prevention/diagnostic rationale 25%, team plan 20%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: Cancer therapy-related immune defects and opportunistic infections
objectives: Relate therapy and immune phenotype to bacterial, fungal, viral and parasitic risk.
Identify when malignancy, drug toxicity, immune-mediated disease or infection may mimic each other.
Use oncology-specific multidisciplinary communication and time-sensitive escalation.
topics: Hematologic malignancy; chemotherapy; targeted and cellular therapies; corticosteroids/biologics; mucositis/lines; neutropenic fever.
boardDomains: Immunocompromised host (5%); internal medicine/noninfectious (18%); bacterial diseases (27%); fungi (5%).
units.casePractice: NCI patient page supports context only; archived IDSA fever/neutropenia guideline is not a current treatment protocol.
units.assessment: Create a therapy-to-risk table with a differential including noninfectious mimics; rubric: immune defect linkage 30%, infection/mimic balance 25%, tests 20%, escalation 25%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: Immunosuppression, pharmacology, interactions and preventive care
objectives: Explain how immunosuppressant mechanisms and recent changes shape net immunosuppression and infection risk.
Recognize clinically important interaction/toxicity themes across anti-infectives and transplant agents.
Outline vaccine, prophylaxis and environmental prevention principles using current authoritative schedules/guidance.
topics: Calcineurin/mTOR inhibitors, antimetabolites, steroids, biologics; pharmacokinetics; prophylaxis; immunization; drug monitoring and toxicity.
units.casePractice: PIDS vaccination modules/slide decks are direct provider links; confirm date and age-group before use. CDC page covers infection-control setting rather than all vaccine schedules.
units.assessment: Interaction-risk map without dosing; rubric: mechanism 25%, interaction/toxicity recognition 30%, prevention rationale 25%, source/date qualifiers 20%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: Infection prevention, stewardship, outbreaks and systems practice
objectives: Apply standard/transmission-based precautions and protective environment concepts appropriately.
Plan surveillance/investigation for suspected healthcare-associated or donor-derived clusters with institutional partners.
Communicate uncertainty, patient-safety actions, equity and transitions of care.
topics: Isolation; environmental control; construction risk; antimicrobial stewardship; outbreak investigation; donor notification; handoff and QI.
boardDomains: Infection prevention/control (5%); internal medicine/noninfectious (18%); antimicrobial therapy (9%).
units.casePractice: CDC isolation page provides clinical setting recommendations; institution-specific policies supersede generic study material. AST webinar supports case discussion only.
units.assessment: Draft a fictional cluster escalation flow; rubric: immediate containment 25%, data/case definition 25%, communication 25%, evaluation/feedback 25%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, consultation synthesis and board-style integration
objectives: Synthesize a focused consult formulation, evidence uncertainty and actionable next questions.
Critically appraise guideline currency, population match, recommendation strength and limitations.
Practice original single-best-answer reasoning across ABIM ID domains while distinguishing general-ID exam from TOID expertise.
topics: Bayesian thinking; guideline appraisal; journal-club methods; consultation note; oral case; transitions; ABIM blueprint weighting and limits.
boardDomains: All ABIM ID categories; particularly immunocompromised host (5%), internal medicine/noninfectious (18%) and infection control (5%).
units.casePractice: ABIM blueprint is public and dated Jan 2026; the 2010/2011 FN and 2016 aspergillosis references require currentness checks.
units.assessment: Prepare 8-minute fictional oral consult plus evidence table; rubric: synthesis 25%, alternative diagnosis 20%, evidence/date appraisal 20%, safe plan/limitations 20%, communication 15%.
units.prerequisites: Physician-level postgraduate ID knowledge; completion of internal medicine residency and baseline infectious diseases fellowship-level study strongly preferred. This is advanced self-study, not an entry-level clinical course.

assignment.title: Integrated fictional consult portfolio
assignment.instructions: Submit a concise consult note, differential/time-risk matrix, diagnostic strategy, source currency table, and team escalation/handoff map for a fictional composite scenario. Do not use actual patient data. No therapy order or dosage is requested. Cite primary sources and label historical/archived recommendations.

rubric.criterion: Evidence currency, uncertainty and guideline fit

assignment.scoring: Each criterion scored 0–4: 0 missing/unsafe, 1 major gaps, 2 partial, 3 sound, 4 nuanced and source-supported. This is formative self-assessment, not validated competence.

assessment.format: 12-unit formative checks; 10 original single-best-answer practice questions; two fictional oral consults; capstone portfolio.
assessment.passingRule: No validated pass threshold. Learner should review any missed objective against current primary guidance and seek faculty feedback. Not an exam predictor or official question bank.
assessment.rubricSummary: Assess reasoning, evidence appraisal, communication and uncertainty—not memorization of outdated recommendations.

studyHours.basis: A transparent study plan (not actual delivered/contact training): 12 units × 5 h (60 h) study, 24 h assignments/case reasoning, 12 h formative questions and review, 24 h source updates/capstone. Counted lecture time remains separate; self-study time does not satisfy clinical training.

mapping.name: Transplant and Oncology Infectious Diseases Fellowship

The extension is not a separate physician specialty or board.

unitMap.text: Pretransplant evaluation, donor assessment and donor-derived infection
coveredTopics: Pretransplant risk review; CMV/EBV/toxo/TB/endemic exposures; donor history/cultures; organ-specific risk; post-transplant notification.

unitMap.text: Diagnostic strategy and test interpretation in immunocompromised hosts
coveredTopics: Blood cultures; tissue/sterile-site sampling; bronchoscopy/BAL; fungal biomarkers; CMV PCR vs tissue disease; radiology/pathology/microbiology integration.

unitMap.text: Fever and neutropenia, bacterial sepsis and antimicrobial stewardship
coveredTopics: Neutropenia; fever; initial stabilization; resistant bacteria; bloodstream/catheter infection; source control; de-escalation and duration.

unitMap.text: SOT organ-specific infection syndromes and post-transplant timeline
coveredTopics: Kidney/urinary and leak; liver/biliary; lung; heart; pancreas/intestine; device and surgical-site infection; time-linked risk.

unitMap.text: CMV, EBV/PTLD and other viral infections in SOT/HCT

unitMap.text: Invasive fungal disease, mold and endemic fungi
coveredTopics: Aspergillus; Mucorales; Candida; Pneumocystis; endemic mycoses; prophylaxis breakthrough; environmental exposure.

unitMap.text: HSCT, leukemia and cellular therapy infection complications
coveredTopics: Autologous/allogeneic HCT; neutropenia; GVHD/steroids; CMV/EBV; mold; Pneumocystis; respiratory viruses; cellular therapy context.

unitMap.text: Cancer therapy-related immune defects and opportunistic infections
coveredTopics: Hematologic malignancy; chemotherapy; targeted and cellular therapies; corticosteroids/biologics; mucositis/lines; neutropenic fever.

unitMap.text: Immunosuppression, pharmacology, interactions and preventive care

unitMap.text: Infection prevention, stewardship, outbreaks and systems practice

unitMap.text: Evidence appraisal, consultation synthesis and board-style integration
coveredTopics: Bayesian thinking; guideline appraisal; journal-club methods; consultation note; oral case; transitions; ABIM blueprint weighting and limits.

topicGaps: 35.4667 of the 36 target specialty video hours remain unfilled after counting one provider-stated 32-minute recording; target minutes and scripts are not rendered hours.

The counted BMT InfoNet talk is patient/caregiver-oriented and introductory; it does not cover advanced clinician decision-making across SOT, HCT, oncology, diagnosis, therapeutics, resistance or stewardship.
The two pre-existing YouTube items remain duration/free-access unverified; speech timestamps do not establish media runtime, so neither is counted.

No additional clinician-level open recording series with verified runtime evidence was found to close the 36-hour floor. The existing 36-hour clip plan, new authored episodes, and appended production targets are all plans/scripts only.

Insufficiently supported topics include organ-specific SOT infection syndromes; oncology and cellular-therapy infections; current fungal and endemic/parasitic guidance; assay-specific diagnostics; anti-infective interactions/toxicity; and current institution-specific stewardship.

medical.boardStatus: No separate ABIM/ABMS Transplant and Oncology Infectious Diseases board examination identified in the ABIM certification menu/policy or the searched public board materials as of 2026-10-07. Hopkins describes TOID as AST-recognized ACGME-equivalent fellowship training. AST curriculum/directory recognition is not board certification. The board mapping below is to the general ABIM ID blueprint only.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Independent education does not confer ABIM internal medicine or ID board eligibility. ABIM ID eligibility ordinarily requires prior ABIM internal medicine certification, qualifying accredited fellowship training, competence/licensure and passing the ID examination; confirm current policy directly with ABIM. Hopkins states TOID applicants should be current or past fellows in good standing in an ACGME-accredited ID fellowship. This course is not eligibility credit.

officialProgrammes.name: Transplant and Oncology Infectious Diseases Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official JH page: clinical TOID fellowship founded 2008; AST recognizes it as ACGME-equivalent; applicants should be current/past ACGME ID fellows in good standing; rotations six months or longer; inpatient consult service, pre-transplant evaluation and continuity clinics; potential research extension up to two years. The extension is not a separate physician specialty or board.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Only exact MED-121 packet offering is Johns Hopkins TOID. The AST opportunity directory contains many institutional postings and “other opportunities”; it is a generic training-opportunity directory, not accreditation/board evidence and not consolidated as variants here. Hopkins TOID is an actual clinical physician fellowship, not research-only. Its research extension is optional and not counted as clinical board specialty. General ACGME ID is a separate 24-month subspecialty; TOID is a focused advanced clinical fellowship/track recognized by AST as equivalent per Hopkins. No separate TOID board exam found. No other exact institutional variant appears in the supplied packet. The PIDS/AST modules are pediatric educational supplements only, not the adult clinical track or a pediatric physician fellowship.
sourceCaveats: This is an independent, unaffiliated educational course; no institutional endorsement or affiliation.
Hopkins reports AST recognition of its programme as ACGME-equivalent; that does not by itself establish an ABMS subspecialty or separate board examination.
ABIM policy and blueprint support general ID certification only; no TOID-specific ABIM exam found in reviewed sources.
ACGME 24-month ID requirements apply to the general ID fellowship, not automatically to the distinct TOID fellowship.
IDSA 2010 febrile neutropenia guideline is archived; aspergillosis guideline page reflects 2016 publication. Confirm current guidance and local protocols.
AST Tx10 is free to add with an AST account; access is gated, and this course does not count it as open public media.
Free slide/video viewing does not grant rights to copy, embed, download, rehost, redistribute or reproduce images. No patient images or records were copied.
The two public YouTube lectures are transcript-discovered, but exact runtime and free playback were not independently verified; therefore 0.0 external video hours are counted.
Human clinical review is NOT PERFORMED. No diagnosis/case volume claim, eligibility promise, pass guarantee, licensure, credential, procedure competence or treatment authorization is made.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 58-year-old with a kidney transplant presents with fever and cough 10 months after transplant. Recent rejection therapy is not in the current medication list. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Assume community-acquired pneumonia because surgery was months ago
Reconstruct recent immunosuppression and exposures while assessing severity and obtaining syndrome-directed evaluation
Diagnose CMV disease from timing alone
Stop all immunosuppression immediately

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current and recent immune state, prophylaxis, exposures and severity shape the differential; calendar time alone is not diagnostic, and medication changes require the transplant team.

practiceQuestions.stem: A donor serology is positive for a latent infection, while the recipient is asymptomatic. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.text: Transmission is certain
Serology alone establishes active donor infection
Use donor/recipient tests and exposure history to inform risk, then apply the appropriate center protocol and follow-up
No action is ever indicated

practiceQuestions.rationale: Serology informs but does not by itself prove active infection or transmission; interpretation depends on test, donor context, recipient and current protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: Several recipients from one donor have unusual early syndromes. What is a key systems step?

options.text: Contact each recipient’s family directly
Notify the transplant center through established donor-derived infection communication pathways
Wait for a culture to prove transmission before notifying anyone
Publish donor identifiers for clinician crowdsourcing

practiceQuestions.rationale: The transplant center/OPO and applicable national processes are the proper formal pathways; privacy and prompt communication matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A transplant recipient has a nonspecific pulmonary infiltrate and negative noninvasive tests. Which principle best guides the next diagnostic discussion?

options.text: A negative screening test excludes infection
Use host, syndrome and pretest probability to select additional sampling and interpret limitations
Treat a biomarker in isolation as definitive
Avoid involving microbiology and radiology

practiceQuestions.rationale: Test limitations and sample quality matter; additional targeted diagnostics and multidisciplinary review may be needed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the ABIM infectious disease examination in relation to TOID training?

options.text: There is a separate ABIM TOID certification exam
The ABIM ID exam covers general infectious disease; no separate TOID board exam was identified in reviewed board materials
Passing the ID exam certifies transplant procedural competence
A Hopkins TOID elective alone confers ID board eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM lists infectious disease certification and a general ID blueprint; the reviewed materials do not list a separate TOID board credential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner uses the linked IDSA neutropenic-fever guideline as a current order set. What is the main flaw?

options.text: The page is archived and guideline is an older 2010 update published in 2011; current local protocols and updated sources are needed
The guideline is a current ACGME requirement
It is intended only for pediatric SOT
It establishes TOID exam eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: The IDSA page marks it archived. It can inform historical concepts but is not a current universal protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best describes the Johns Hopkins programme from its official page?

options.text: A stand-alone board certification
A clinical TOID fellowship with an AST-recognized ACGME-equivalent designation, requiring prior ID fellowship standing as stated on the programme page
A research-only postdoc with no clinical training
A pediatric ID residency

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins identifies it as clinical training and states AST recognizes it as ACGME-equivalent; applicants should be current or past ID fellows in good standing in ACGME-accredited ID training.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an immunocompromised host, why can a classic clinical presentation be less reliable?

options.text: Immune suppression can alter inflammatory responses and presentation
Transplant eliminates infection risk
All diagnostic tests are falsely positive
Fever is always absent

practiceQuestions.rationale: Host immune deficits and therapies can modify presentation; evaluate the entire syndrome and test context.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the appropriate use of a freely linked PIDS transplant teaching slide deck?

options.text: Copy its images into a new public course because the link is free
Link to the provider resource and respect its terms; do not assume free viewing allows republication
Treat it as adult board blueprint
Claim all embedded clinical images are public domain

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free access is not a rehosting license; pediatric scope and any image rights must be respected.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the strongest learning outcome for a fictional donor-derived infection exercise?

options.text: Name a single organism without evidence
Practice structured donor data review, cautious inference, and formal communication/escalation
Predict which organ will be infected
Calculate a case-volume credential

practiceQuestions.rationale: The educational objective is disciplined evidence review and systems communication, avoiding unsupported certainty or invented outcomes.

unitMap.text: Foundations: history, examination, optics and test interpretation
Acute vision loss, red eye and urgent triage
Lens, cataract, pseudophakia and refractive care
Cornea, external disease and anterior segment
Glaucoma and optic neuropathy
Retina, vitreous, macula and intraocular tumors
Pediatric ophthalmology and strabismus
Neuro-ophthalmology
Uveitis, ocular inflammation and systemic disease
Oculofacial, orbit and lacrimal disorders
Ocular pharmacology, systemic disease, safety and ethics
Integrated oral-board style patient-management reasoning

topicGaps: The only newly verified long-form series is the University of Iowa glaucoma curriculum. Glaucoma now has substantial free recorded coverage, but it is an introductory, 2015-version resource rather than a full residency course and does not supply current clinician-reviewed recommendations.

The total verified free video ledger is 16.635 hours, leaving 19.365 hours below the 36-hour target. The extra 50 Iowa recordings contribute 11.698 hours; original AAO recordings contribute 4.937 hours. Original-script target minutes are planned production only, not watched, rendered or counted hours.

Insufficient video depth remains across cornea/external disease, cataract and refractive optics, retina/macula and retinal tumors, uveitis, pediatric/strabismus beyond introductory coverage, oculofacial/orbit/lacrimal, neuro-ophthalmology, ocular pathology/genetics, systemic disease/pharmacology, imaging interpretation, evidence appraisal and oral patient-management. The Iowa glaucoma video set does not remediate these non-glaucoma domains.

Harvard public curriculum pages do not expose the internal lecture schedule or a public recorded curriculum. The source review found other ophthalmology course/lecture collections but did not count them where the exact media runtime, free watchability, or independent non-duplicate recording could not be verified. Mayo Clinic Grand Rounds is advertised as free viewing, but its LMS pages list episode materials as locked and registration controls, so those videos were excluded rather than accessed through an account.

Iowa Glaucoma Curriculum states 50 chapters and just under 12 hours. The ledger uses the 50 individually named chapters whose respective public pages display a duration; its un-timed preface is separately disclosed and excluded. Course chapter pages identify version 1.0 dated 2015-09-28 unless updated, so date-sensitive pharmacology and management claims must be cross-checked against current guidance.
Automated source and ledger review only. Human clinician review has not been performed.

boardNames: American Board of Ophthalmology (ABO) — general ophthalmology initial certification
medical.boardStatus: A distinct US physician specialty with ABO certification following accredited residency training, licensure, Written Qualifying Examination and Oral Examination. ABMS currently lists the American Board of Ophthalmology specialty certificate and no ABO subspecialty certificates; this does not rule out non-ABMS fellowship credentials. Harvard-listed fellowships are not distinct ABO board exams.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study course confers no medical degree, ACGME credit, accredited training, license, board eligibility, board certification or procedure competence and cannot guarantee exam performance. The ABO requires qualifying accredited training and licensure plus its examinations.

officialProgrammes.institution: Harvard Ophthalmology / Mass Eye and Ear
officialProgrammes.name: Harvard Ophthalmology Residency Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official four-year integrated physician residency (PGY-1 transitional year plus ophthalmology training); requires the Newton-Wellesley Transitional Year Internship, with three months at Mass Eye and Ear in PGY-1. Site names seven teaching hospitals: Newton-Wellesley Hospital; Massachusetts Eye and Ear; Massachusetts General Hospital; Brigham and Women’s Hospital; Boston Children’s Hospital; Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; Veterans Affairs Boston Healthcare System. Most time at Mass Eye and Ear. Public page describes surgery/simulation and elective, but does not publish a complete rotation schedule or didactic library. Exact institutional variant preserved.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The assigned item is the Harvard Ophthalmology / Mass Eye and Ear integrated clinical physician residency, not an institutional directory category, generic course, optometry track, research postdoctoral fellowship or combined residency. The official programme’s non-identical sites/affiliates are preserved in the programme note. Harvard-affiliated fellowships listed in program statistics are not merged into this residency curriculum. The curriculum page exposes PGY year headings, not a detailed public schedule.
sourceCaveats: ABO WQE outline is current for 2026 per board source. Oral exam outline source states update December 2020; check for updates before use.

Harvard program website is programme self-description, not independent accreditation or full curriculum audit. Current ACGME requirements support specialty-level framework but do not establish Harvard-specific curriculum details.
Harvard program-by-numbers contains historic aggregate visit data from 2022 and surgical averages from AY 2024–25; not guarantees, requirements or individual outcomes.
Clinical guideline pages may be updated and may restrict full-text access; check current source before relying on any recommendation. No clinical review performed.

AAO lecture pages show duration in a public listing, but content is copyright-protected. The video ledger records runtime/access from source webpage and distinct embedded asset identifiers; it does not imply a redistribution license.
Moran CORE content and clinical images remain copyrighted; free-to-view is not rehost permission. No patient data or image copied.
The course and original questions are not official ABO exam material, validated exam prep or a pass predictor.

sourceReferences.title: ABO WQE Content Outline (effective 2026)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Nine domain weights: lens/cataract 13%, cornea/external/anterior segment 13%, glaucoma 14%, neuro-ophthalmology 10%, oculofacial/orbit 10%, pediatric/strabismus 10%, refractive/optics 8%, retina/vitreous/tumors 15%, uveitis 8%; four care dimensions and cross-cutting subjects.

topicGaps: The only newly verified long-form series is the University of Iowa glaucoma curriculum. Glaucoma now has substantial free recorded coverage, but it is an introductory, 2015-version resource rather than a full residency course and does not supply current clinician-reviewed recommendations.

The total verified free video ledger is 16.635 hours, leaving 19.365 hours below the 36-hour target. The extra 50 Iowa recordings contribute 11.698 hours; original AAO recordings contribute 4.937 hours. Original-script target minutes are planned production only, not watched, rendered or counted hours.

Insufficient video depth remains across cornea/external disease, cataract and refractive optics, retina/macula and retinal tumors, uveitis, pediatric/strabismus beyond introductory coverage, oculofacial/orbit/lacrimal, neuro-ophthalmology, ocular pathology/genetics, systemic disease/pharmacology, imaging interpretation, evidence appraisal and oral patient-management. The Iowa glaucoma video set does not remediate these non-glaucoma domains.

Harvard public curriculum pages do not expose the internal lecture schedule or a public recorded curriculum. The source review found other ophthalmology course/lecture collections but did not count them where the exact media runtime, free watchability, or independent non-duplicate recording could not be verified. Mayo Clinic Grand Rounds is advertised as free viewing, but its LMS pages list episode materials as locked and registration controls, so those videos were excluded rather than accessed through an account.

Iowa Glaucoma Curriculum states 50 chapters and just under 12 hours. The ledger uses the 50 individually named chapters whose respective public pages display a duration; its un-timed preface is separately disclosed and excluded. Course chapter pages identify version 1.0 dated 2015-09-28 unless updated, so date-sensitive pharmacology and management claims must be cross-checked against current guidance.
Automated source and ledger review only. Human clinician review has not been performed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient reports sudden painless monocular visual loss. Which first step best structures evaluation?

options.text: Assume retinal detachment and schedule routine follow-up
Clarify onset/course and associated symptoms, compare acuity/fields/pupils, perform focused exam and arrange urgency based on findings
Treat presumed optic neuritis without examination
Wait for symptoms to resolve

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO acute vision-loss lecture teaches focused history, differential and recognition of situations needing urgent action; symptom description alone does not establish etiology.

options.text: Reassure because conjunctivitis is most common
Treat as potentially vision-threatening; obtain focused history/exam and urgent ophthalmic assessment
Start steroid drops without cause assessment
Use redness alone to diagnose allergy

practiceQuestions.rationale: Red-eye assessment should recognize danger signs; pain, vision reduction and pupil abnormalities are concerning rather than diagnostic by themselves.

title: Medical Retina Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent self-study curriculum; not clinical training)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Completed medical school and ophthalmology residency or equivalent; intended learner level is ophthalmology-trained physician/fellow.
Baseline retinal examination and ophthalmic imaging literacy; this course does not teach supervised examination/procedure performance.
Ability to read primary literature and current practice guidelines; verify local laws and current prescribing information.
objectives: Synthesize symptoms, exam, and multimodal imaging into a retina differential while separating observation from inference.
Explain diagnosis and management evidence for AMD, DR/DME, RVO, RAO, inherited disease, inflammation, chorioretinal tumors, and vitreoretinal-interface disease.
Identify urgent systemic or ocular escalation pathways, risks and evidence limitations.
Interpret major retina imaging modalities and communicate technical limitations.
Critically appraise retina research and counsel about uncertainty, privacy, and rights.
Map selected content to the current ABO WQE domains without claiming board examination equivalence or readiness.

units.title: Retinal anatomy, physiology, and clinicopathologic localization
objectives: Relate retinal layers, RPE, choroid, and vitreoretinal interface to symptoms and structural OCT.
Localize pathology by fundus/OCT findings and build a differential before naming a disease.
topics: Retinal layers; macula/periphery; circulation; barrier; photoreceptors; anatomy-to-OCT mapping.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors; Pathophysiology / Basic Science
units.casePractice: Create a labeled layer-to-OCT concept map and explain 3 localization decisions.
units.assessment: Reasoning rubric (0–4): correct anatomic localization 40%, evidence 30%, alternatives 20%, uncertainty 10%.

units.title: Multimodal imaging and diagnostic reasoning
objectives: Select and interpret OCT, color fundus, FAF, FA/ICGA, ultrasound, and electrophysiology by clinical question.
Distinguish image artifact from true fluid, atrophy, neovascular complex, or inflammation; state what imaging cannot prove.
topics: OCT segmentation; IRF/SRF/sub-RPE material; angiography phases; FAF patterns; ultrasound; ERG; multimodal concordance.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Diagnostic Testing
units.casePractice: Submit 5 image-reading worksheets using linked educational examples (no images rehosted).
units.assessment: Rubric: observation separate from inference (30%), modality choice (25%), differential (25%), limitations (20%).

units.title: Age-related macular degeneration: phenotype, risk, and prevention
objectives: Stage non-neovascular AMD and recognize signs suggesting exudation/atrophy.
Apply evidence-supported counseling and describe the boundaries of AREDS2 and genetic testing.
topics: Drusen/pigment; intermediate AMD; geographic atrophy; smoking; AREDS/AREDS2 eligibility; home monitoring; OCT and FAF.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Macular Diseases
units.casePractice: Write a one-page comparison of surveillance options by stage, with a cited source and uncertainty note.
units.assessment: Rubric: stage correctly (35%), counseling matches guideline (35%), no unsupported supplement claims (20%), citations (10%).

units.title: Neovascular AMD and anti-VEGF decision frameworks
objectives: Identify activity and differential of macular neovascularization using history and multimodal imaging.
Compare first-line anti-VEGF strategy concepts, monitoring, response, recurrence, and treatment risks without prescribing.
topics: New symptoms; OCT/FA; type 1/2/3 MNV; pachychoroid mimics; loading/maintenance concepts; treat-and-extend vs PRN evidence; endophthalmitis warning signs.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Macular Diseases; Management / Outcomes
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional serial OCT vignette and defend what additional data would change interpretation.
units.assessment: Rubric: activity evidence 35%, alternatives 25%, monitoring logic 25%, safety/limits 15%.

units.title: Diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema
objectives: Classify NPDR/PDR and DME using clinical descriptions and OCT; distinguish severity from symptoms.
Compare anti-VEGF, PRP, observation, and systemic risk control at guideline level and identify urgent referral considerations.
topics: Screening; ETDRS severity concepts; center-involved DME; PDR; PRP; anti-VEGF; pregnancy/puberty; systemic risk and rapid glycemic change.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Retinal Vascular Diseases; Pediatric retinal disorders where applicable
units.casePractice: Create a treatment-options matrix for 4 fictional DR/DME profiles; do not prescribe to real people.
units.assessment: Rubric: phenotype/severity 30%, evidence-based options 30%, patient/system context 20%, safety and caveat 20%.

units.title: Retinal vein occlusion and other venous disease
objectives: Differentiate BRVO, CRVO, hemi-CRVO and ischemic risk features; recognize macular edema and neovascular complications.
Integrate ocular care with systemic vascular-risk assessment and follow-up.
topics: Fundus/OCT/FA; macular edema; anti-VEGF; steroid risks; laser role; NVI/NVG; systemic risk discussion.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Retinal Vascular Diseases
units.casePractice: Interpret a constructed RVO timeline and list ocular and systemic issues requiring clinician coordination.
units.assessment: Rubric: classification 30%, complications 30%, treatment evidence 25%, coordination/safety 15%.

units.title: Retinal arterial occlusion and acute-care interface
objectives: Treat symptomatic CRAO/BRAO/OAO as a time-critical systemic vascular event in clinical reasoning.
Identify when older-age GCA assessment is essential and distinguish established referral from unproven ocular rescue therapy.
topics: Acute symptom timing; stroke-center referral; embolic-source workup; GCA; age-specific differential; limited evidence for post-acute vision-restoring therapy.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Retinal Vascular Diseases; emergency and patient safety
units.casePractice: Write a 60-second simulated handoff using only fictional details and current referral guidance.
units.assessment: Rubric: urgency/referral 40%, systemic differential 25%, GCA qualifier 20%, no unproven treatment claim 15%.

units.title: Inherited retinal disease, toxic retinopathy, and precision diagnosis
objectives: Use phenotype, family history, multimodal imaging, and electrophysiology to frame inherited retinal disease differential.
State molecular confirmation and indication limits for gene-directed therapy.
topics: Rod-cone/cone-rod patterns; phenocopies; ERG; genetic counseling/testing; RPE65 biallelic confirmation; toxicity patterns; trial literacy.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Inherited Retinal and Choroidal Disease
units.casePractice: Build a fictional phenotype-first differential and a genetic-testing question list.
units.assessment: Rubric: phenotype 30%, differential 25%, test utility/limitations 25%, therapy indication boundary 20%.

units.title: Inflammatory, infectious, and white-dot posterior segment disease
objectives: Recognize posterior uveitis/white-dot pattern families and develop a differential that includes infection and masquerade.
Choose workup concepts guided by phenotype, systemic context, and urgency; avoid immunosuppression assumptions.
topics: White-dot syndromes; infectious retinitis; posterior/panuveitis; imaging; systemic workup; treatment risk framing.
boardDomains: Uveitis; Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors
units.casePractice: Create a differential tree from a fictional photopsia/scotoma vignette; identify missing data before narrowing.
units.assessment: Rubric: differential breadth 30%, red flags 25%, workup reasoning 25%, uncertainty 20%.

units.title: Chorioretinal lesions, tumors, myopia, and pachychoroid mimics
objectives: Distinguish benign nevus surveillance concepts from features that warrant ocular oncology evaluation.
Compare myopic degeneration, CSC, and secondary CNV patterns without over-relying on one sign.
topics: Choroidal nevus/melanoma red flags; imaging modalities; pathologic myopia; CSC; secondary CNV; differential.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Intraocular Tumors; Macular Diseases
units.casePractice: Submit a structured descriptive report for fictional lesions and justify referral/monitoring questions.
units.assessment: Rubric: description 30%, differential 25%, appropriate escalation 25%, avoid diagnosis certainty 20%.

units.title: Vitreoretinal interface, peripheral retina, and urgent symptoms
objectives: Recognize symptomatic PVD, tear/detachment warning patterns, vitreomacular traction, ERM, and macular hole.
Distinguish educational triage from procedure training; identify urgent in-person evaluation needs.
topics: Flashes/floaters/curtain; Shafer sign concept; peripheral lesions; OCT interface; detachment referral; medical-vs-surgical scope.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors: Vitreous and Peripheral Retinal Abnormalities; Trauma
units.casePractice: Create a referral-priority rubric for fictional symptoms and explain which findings require dilated exam.
units.assessment: Rubric: red-flag recognition 40%, differential 25%, time-sensitive escalation 25%, scope 10%.

units.title: Clinical scholarship, evidence appraisal, ethics, and quality
objectives: Critically appraise retina trial design, outcomes, external validity, adverse events, and conflicts.
Communicate uncertainty, protect privacy, and present source-linked cases without copying protected data or images.
topics: Landmark-study literacy; endpoints; bias; guideline date/version; consent/de-identification; patient communication; quality/safety.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors; Ethics / Professionalism; Patient Safety / Quality
units.casePractice: Journal-club brief on an open paper and a 5-minute fictional case talk; no identifiable records.
units.assessment: Rubric: design/evidence 35%, applicability 25%, uncertainty 20%, privacy/source practice 20%.

assignment.title: Capstone: fictional multimodal retina case conference
assignment.instructions: Write a structured 1,500–2,000 word educational case analysis using an explicitly fictional vignette. Provide problem representation, prioritized differential, image-description checklist (use textual schematic only or link to an authorized case), diagnostic evidence needed, guideline-based options and limits, urgent referral flags, and one-page evidence appraisal. No patient data/images; no prescription or unsupervised procedure plan.

assessment.format: 12 original formative MCQs plus unit short submissions, journal club, and capstone; no official ABO item reproduction.
assessment.passingRule: No validated pass threshold. Suggested self-study completion means answer explanations reviewed and all assignments submitted, not clinical competence or predicted exam success.
assessment.validityNotice: Questions are original educational exercises, not psychometrically validated, official exam items, or predictors of passing.

studyHours.plan: A learner-paced 120-hour PLAN: 36 target external video hours (currently 19.9164 observed hours plus 16.0836-hour production gap), 36 hours reading, 24 hours image/case reasoning, 16 hours questions and review, 8 hours capstone. Study hours are an estimate of planned effort, not observed media or clinical training.

unitMap.text: Retinal anatomy, physiology, and clinicopathologic localization
coveredTopics: Retinal layers; macula/periphery; circulation; barrier; photoreceptors; anatomy-to-OCT mapping.

unitMap.text: Multimodal imaging and diagnostic reasoning
coveredTopics: OCT segmentation; IRF/SRF/sub-RPE material; angiography phases; FAF patterns; ultrasound; ERG; multimodal concordance.

unitMap.text: Age-related macular degeneration: phenotype, risk, and prevention
coveredTopics: Drusen/pigment; intermediate AMD; geographic atrophy; smoking; AREDS/AREDS2 eligibility; home monitoring; OCT and FAF.

unitMap.text: Neovascular AMD and anti-VEGF decision frameworks
coveredTopics: New symptoms; OCT/FA; type 1/2/3 MNV; pachychoroid mimics; loading/maintenance concepts; treat-and-extend vs PRN evidence; endophthalmitis warning signs.

unitMap.text: Diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema
coveredTopics: Screening; ETDRS severity concepts; center-involved DME; PDR; PRP; anti-VEGF; pregnancy/puberty; systemic risk and rapid glycemic change.

unitMap.text: Retinal vein occlusion and other venous disease
coveredTopics: Fundus/OCT/FA; macular edema; anti-VEGF; steroid risks; laser role; NVI/NVG; systemic risk discussion.

unitMap.text: Retinal arterial occlusion and acute-care interface
coveredTopics: Acute symptom timing; stroke-center referral; embolic-source workup; GCA; age-specific differential; limited evidence for post-acute vision-restoring therapy.

unitMap.text: Inherited retinal disease, toxic retinopathy, and precision diagnosis
coveredTopics: Rod-cone/cone-rod patterns; phenocopies; ERG; genetic counseling/testing; RPE65 biallelic confirmation; toxicity patterns; trial literacy.

unitMap.text: Inflammatory, infectious, and white-dot posterior segment disease
coveredTopics: White-dot syndromes; infectious retinitis; posterior/panuveitis; imaging; systemic workup; treatment risk framing.

unitMap.text: Chorioretinal lesions, tumors, myopia, and pachychoroid mimics
coveredTopics: Choroidal nevus/melanoma red flags; imaging modalities; pathologic myopia; CSC; secondary CNV; differential.

unitMap.text: Vitreoretinal interface, peripheral retina, and urgent symptoms
coveredTopics: Flashes/floaters/curtain; Shafer sign concept; peripheral lesions; OCT interface; detachment referral; medical-vs-surgical scope.

unitMap.text: Clinical scholarship, evidence appraisal, ethics, and quality
coveredTopics: Landmark-study literacy; endpoints; bias; guideline date/version; consent/de-identification; patient communication; quality/safety.

topicGaps: The 36.0000-hour external-video floor is met: 38.1731 unique, free, observed hours (137423 observed seconds); 2.1731 hours above the floor. Written scripts/target minutes do not contribute to these hours.

Still thin at physician-fellow depth: acute retinal arterial occlusion/stroke and GCA decisions; infectious/posterior uveitis and masquerade discrimination; tumor/lesion referral; detailed ERG interpretation and genetic-test counseling. The video ledger includes broad resident-level coverage, but these domains require primary-guideline/board-blueprint study and supervised teaching.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Not a credentialing path and does not confer board eligibility. Official MEE page requires applicants to be board eligible in ophthalmology, to have completed an ACGME-accredited ophthalmology residency or equivalent, passed USMLE parts I–III, and hold a full medical license. Confirm current eligibility with the institution and ABO.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass Eye and Ear (Harvard-affiliated teaching hospital)
officialProgrammes.name: Medical Retina Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme describes a one-year fellowship starting July, one fellow accepted per year, San Francisco Match #4845; broad retina/vitreous/choroid clinical exposure, imaging (FA/ICG, ultrasound, OCT, autofluorescence, ERG), laser exposure, retina clinics, conferences, resident teaching and mentored research. Eligibility listed as board-eligible ophthalmology, ACGME residency or equivalent, USMLE I–III, full medical license. The page does not state ACGME fellowship accreditation or AUPO FCC compliance; this is not inferred.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One exact institution variant in packet: Mass Eye and Ear Medical Retina Fellowship. This is a physician clinical fellowship, not a residency, generic directory label, research-only postdoctoral job, or combined retina-surgery program. A separate vitreoretinal surgery fellowship exists at MEE and is not merged. Harvard-affiliated MEE is institution context, not an affiliation of this independent course.
sourceCaveats: Official programme pages provide a selective public summary and do not expose internal conference materials, full rotation calendars, case volumes, assessment outcomes, or all didactics.

MEE page does not state ACGME fellowship accreditation. AUPO FCC is voluntary compliance; current MEE compliant status could not be confirmed because public listing sends users to SF Match after registration.
ABO is the ophthalmology board; no separate medical retina board exam was identified in checked official sources. Not proof that no other optional society recognition exists.
Clinical guideline pages can be updated; AAO AMD and RVO PPP pages note June 2026 updates. Clinical guidance needs human specialist review before publication or use.
No human clinical review has been performed; no diagnosis, treatment order, dose, or real-patient advice is supplied.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees new distortion in a fictional older adult with known AMD and new subretinal fluid on OCT. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Conclude neovascular AMD from the OCT alone
Integrate symptoms, prior images, examination and appropriate multimodal evaluation
Assume the finding is artifact
Recommend a supplement regardless of AMD stage

practiceQuestions.rationale: OCT findings require clinical context and multimodal assessment; new distortion merits prompt eye-doctor evaluation. Do not diagnose from one sign.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which counseling statement best reflects current AAO AMD guidance?

options.text: Routine genetic testing is recommended for all AMD
Smoking cessation should be discussed; routine genetic testing is not currently recommended
AREDS2 is proven for all early AMD and unaffected relatives
Early AMD requires anti-VEGF injections

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current AAO PPP recommends smoking cessation and says routine genetic testing is not recommended; supplementation is stage-specific, not universal.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with diabetes has center-involved DME on imaging but good acuity. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Anti-VEGF always must begin immediately regardless of acuity
AAO guidance allows treatment to be deferred in selected center-involved DME eyes with good VA until VA is affected, with clinician monitoring
PRP is the only effective option
OCT alone determines the full plan

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO DR PPP states that in CI-DME with good visual acuity, treatment may reasonably be deferred until acuity is affected (20/30 or worse); individualized clinician assessment/monitoring remains essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional symptomatic patient has an acute retinal artery occlusion. What system-level response is recommended?

options.text: Routine follow-up in several months
Immediate referral to nearest stroke referral center for prompt assessment
Treat as isolated eye disease only
Wait for OCT to normalize before referral

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO retinal/ophthalmic artery occlusion PPP recommends immediate stroke-center referral and systemic evaluation; this is a time-sensitive emergency pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a patient older than 50 with retinal artery occlusion, what additional diagnosis must be considered?

options.text: Giant cell arteritis
Retinopathy of prematurity
Macular telangiectasia only
Acute angle closure

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO PPP advises considering GCA in patients >50; clinical evaluation is urgent when suspected.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which clinical distinction about CRAO treatment is supported by the AAO PPP?

options.text: A proven therapy reverses established post-acute vision loss
After acute phase, no proven treatment reverses vision loss; evidence is insufficient for IV/intra-arterial fibrinolytics
PRP is proven to restore central acuity
Anti-VEGF is a substitute for stroke assessment

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO PPP explicitly notes no proven post-acute vision-restoring treatment and insufficient evidence for antifibrinolytics.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional RVO case with macular edema, what does the updated AAO PPP identify as first-line treatment class?

options.text: Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents
Oral antibiotics
Immediate retinal detachment surgery
No treatment in every case

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026-updated AAO RVO PPP identifies anti-VEGF as first-line for associated macular edema; choices remain a clinician-patient decision.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which concern is particularly associated with CRVO/hemi-CRVO relative to BRVO in AAO guidance?

options.text: Higher anterior-segment neovascularization/neovascular glaucoma risk
No glaucoma relationship
Lower ischemia in every case
No macular edema

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO RVO PPP notes CRVO/hemi-CRVO association with glaucoma and higher risk of anterior segment neovascularization/NVG than BRVO.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the FDA-approved indication for LUXTURNA?

options.text: Any inherited retinal degeneration
Confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy
All dry AMD
Any patient with a poor ERG

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA product information limits the indication to patients with confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy.

practiceQuestions.stem: An investigator wants to reuse an EyeRounds retinal image in a paid commercial course. Which is correct?

options.text: Educational viewing means free commercial reuse
EyeRounds allows limited personal/noncommercial educational use subject to attribution and image integrity; financial gain requires written authorization
Images may be altered and reposted if source is cited
Images are public domain

practiceQuestions.rationale: EyeRounds terms allow personal or educational use with intact attribution and restrictions; no financial-gain reuse without written permission. Link rather than rehost where uncertain.

practiceQuestions.stem: A retina image is publicly viewable in the ASRS Retina Image Bank. Can a course assume that download and republication are licensed?

options.text: Yes, open access means public domain
No; viewability does not itself provide a reuse/rehosting license; link and check item-specific permissions
Yes, if patient name is cropped
Yes, for any commercial purpose

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASRS describes an open-access image bank but its landing page does not grant a blanket republication license. Follow item-level terms/permissions; do not copy images into this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: What credential is established by the Medical Retina Fellowship itself?

options.text: An independent medical-retina board certificate
A state medical license
No separate board credential is established by this independent self-study; the ABO certifies ophthalmology, and AUPO FCC is a voluntary fellowship compliance framework
Guaranteed ABO exam eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO is the US ophthalmology certifying board; AUPO FCC describes voluntary fellowship compliance. MEE page identifies clinical fellowship eligibility and duration, not a separate retina board exam or guaranteed certification.

title: Ophthalmology Residency Program
prerequisites: Intended for advanced independent study by learners with medical-school-level biomedical and clinical foundations; not an entry route to physician training.
Anatomy/physiology, basic optics, pathology, epidemiology, evidence appraisal and general clinical terminology are assumed; unit 1 provides review.
Clinical knowledge must be checked against current AAO/ABO and specialty sources. Some freely linked archive lectures are historical (2020/2022) and do not substitute for updated guidelines.
Do not examine, diagnose, treat, prescribe, perform procedures, handle real patient data, or act clinically based on this course.
objectives: Map course study to the current publicly published ABO WQE domain weights and oral-exam categories without implying exam equivalence.
Explain anatomy, optics and evidence-based reasoning across anterior segment, glaucoma, retina, neuro-ophthalmology, uveitis, oculofacial and pediatric ophthalmology.
Use a safe case-presentation format that distinguishes symptom, observation, differential, evidence and uncertainty.
Identify when current source review and supervised professional judgment are required.
Evaluate public images and recordings without copying protected materials or patient information.

units.title: Visual system foundations, examination logic and optical anatomy
objectives: Relate cornea, lens, retina, optic nerve and visual pathway anatomy to symptom localization.
Describe a systematic ophthalmic history/examination sequence and distinguish observation from inference.
Explain basic image formation, refraction, accommodation, visual acuity and visual-field concepts.
topics: Visual pathways and ocular anatomy
Acuity, pupils, fields, motility, anterior segment and fundus examination concepts
Optics and imaging fundamentals; evidence and uncertainty
units.casePractice: Use a fictional symptom-to-anatomic-localization vignette; state what additional exam data are needed and what cannot be inferred from one finding.
units.assessment: Annotated eye-anatomy diagram and short structured examination-plan worksheet.

units.title: Cornea, external disease and anterior segment
objectives: Build a differential for corneal opacity, pain, photophobia and red eye from history and slit-lamp descriptors.
Distinguish infectious, immune-mediated, traumatic/toxic and degenerative categories while flagging time-critical threats.
Explain why contact-lens history, epithelial integrity and anterior chamber findings change urgency.
topics: Corneal anatomy/pathology; surface disease; keratitis and ulcer patterns
Conjunctival/scleral disorders; trauma, exposure, and diagnostic-test limitations
boardDomains: Cornea, External Disease, and Anterior Segment (13%)
units.casePractice: Compare fictional red-eye summaries and justify a differential and escalation threshold without prescribing.
units.assessment: Eight-item pattern-recognition quiz plus a differential that lists a dangerous alternative.

units.title: Lens, cataract, aphakia and pseudophakia
objectives: Classify lens opacity and relate lens/capsular anatomy to visual symptoms.
Recognize systemic, traumatic, congenital, drug-associated and post-procedural contexts.
Explain IOL and pseudophakic complication concepts without attempting surgical planning.
topics: Lens embryology, pathology, cataract and IOLs
Aphakia, pseudophakia, capsular bag and complication reasoning
units.casePractice: Classify an explicitly fictional cataract case and make a problem representation; distinguish educational discussion from consent or surgical care.
units.assessment: Lens morphology and mechanism concept map with sources.

units.title: Glaucoma: diagnosis, structure/function and secondary causes
objectives: Integrate optic nerve appearance, gonioscopy, visual fields and OCT as complementary evidence.
Differentiate open-angle, angle-closure and secondary glaucoma mechanisms at a conceptual level.
Explain why IOP alone neither establishes nor excludes glaucomatous damage.
topics: Glaucoma suspect and primary/secondary glaucoma; pediatric overlap
Structural-functional concordance, progression and measurement limitations
Current clinical practice cross-check against current AAO PPP
units.casePractice: Label findings as structural, functional, risk, or confounder in a fictional longitudinal data set.
units.assessment: Short oral case defense with an uncertainty statement and source/date check.

units.title: Retina, vitreous, vascular and macular disease
objectives: Localize common retinal symptoms and interpret the limits of fundus/OCT/angiographic evidence.
Distinguish vascular, macular, vitreous and peripheral retinal problem categories.
Recognize flashes/floaters/curtain symptoms as requiring timely professional evaluation; avoid false reassurance.
topics: Retinal anatomy and pathology; macular/vascular/choroidal conditions
Vitreous and peripheral retinal abnormalities, retinal breaks/detachment, ocular trauma
Diabetic retinopathy, age-related and inherited disease concepts
units.casePractice: Use a fictional photopsia/floaters stem to identify the key missing data, urgent differential and need for a real examination.
units.assessment: Three-stage vignette: problem representation, differential, evidence/limitation note.

units.title: Uveitis, scleritis and masquerade reasoning
objectives: Classify intraocular inflammation by anatomic location, course and laterality.
Generate infectious, noninfectious and masquerade differential categories from supplied fictional clues.
Explain why immunosuppression cannot be considered without infection exclusion and clinician supervision.
topics: Anterior, intermediate, posterior and panuveitis
Infectious/noninfectious etiologies; pediatric overlap; scleritis; masquerade syndromes
units.casePractice: Sort fictional findings into anatomic localization, urgency, infection risk and tests requiring a supervising clinician.
units.assessment: Differential-and-test rationale rubric; no patient treatment instructions.

units.title: Neuro-ophthalmology, pupils, fields, motility and pain
objectives: Localize a visual-field, pupil or ocular-motor abnormality to plausible afferent/efferent pathway levels.
Differentiate optic disc edema from other disc appearances conceptually and articulate diagnostic uncertainty.
Recognize symptom patterns where neurologic/systemic assessment is time-sensitive.
topics: Optic neuropathy, papilledema, diplopia, nystagmus and pupillary disorders
Visual fields, headache/eye pain and imaging; functional visual loss as a positive diagnosis only after appropriate assessment
units.casePractice: Localize fictional pupil, field and motility findings separately; list dangerous alternatives and information needed before any diagnosis.
units.assessment: Localization worksheet plus five short oral questions.

units.title: Oculofacial plastics, eyelids, lacrimal system and orbit
objectives: Describe a structured approach to lid, lacrimal and orbital symptoms/findings.
Distinguish broad inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, traumatic and neurologic categories.
Identify vision- and life-threatening orbit patterns requiring urgent specialist assessment.
topics: Eyelid anatomy/pathology, ptosis and adnexal lesions
Orbit pathology, orbital imaging, lacrimal drainage and oculofacial principles
units.casePractice: For a fictional unilateral proptosis scenario, identify history/exam gaps, the urgent differential, and limits of an image-only exercise.
units.assessment: Problem representation and escalation rationale scored for safety and evidence.

units.title: Pediatric ophthalmology, amblyopia, strabismus and congenital disease
objectives: Explain visual development and amblyopia risk in age-sensitive terms.
Describe strabismus/alignment and nystagmus concepts and connect them to referral-level reasoning.
Identify leukocoria, acute visual behavior change and pediatric ocular emergencies as prompt evaluation concerns.
topics: Pediatric anterior and posterior segment, retina and glaucoma
Sensory/motor physiology, strabismus, amblyopia, nystagmus, ocular manifestations of systemic disease
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional child with an abnormal red reflex or new deviation; name urgent concerns without making a real-patient diagnosis.
units.assessment: Pediatric case comparison and developmental rationale.

units.title: Refraction, optics, visual physiology and low-vision concepts
objectives: Apply lens/sign conventions and basic optical principles to conceptual refractive examples.
Differentiate refractive error from ocular/neural causes of reduced acuity.
Discuss visual function/low vision as part of patient-centered care without offering an individualized prescription.
topics: Refraction and accommodation; optics; visual physiology; contact lens/refractive surgery concepts
Instrumentation, low-vision and test limitations
units.casePractice: Solve fictional optics sign-convention and acuity-localization problems; distinguish optical blur from retinal/optic-nerve concern.
units.assessment: Calculation/concept worksheet with method and units.

units.title: Ocular tumors, pathology, ultrasonography and multimodal interpretation
objectives: Organize intraocular/orbital mass differentials by location and age/context.
Explain the role and limits of ocular ultrasonography when the fundus is obscured.
Use pathology/imaging as supporting evidence rather than a stand-alone diagnosis.
topics: Intraocular and orbital tumors; ocular pathology; ultrasound basics
Differential diagnosis, image limitations, referral and multidisciplinary review
units.casePractice: Compare fictional lesion locations and identify which imaging modality can answer which question; no copied patient images.
units.assessment: Short multimodal-case memo including alternative diagnoses and evidence limits.

units.title: Integrated board-style reasoning, safety, ethics and quality
objectives: Structure answers around presentation, diagnostic tests, management/outcomes/complications, and pathophysiology/risk.
Communicate uncertainty, red flags, handoff and need for supervised care.
Distinguish published board scope from training requirements and current clinical guidelines.
topics: ABO cross-domain WQE tasks and oral case format; patient safety, diagnostic error, ethics, communication, QI, team-based care
Critical appraisal, guideline date checking, image provenance and copyright
boardDomains: Cross-cutting WQE domains: presentation; diagnostic testing; management/outcomes/complications/prognosis; pathophysiology/basic science/histology/epidemiology/risk assessment
Patient safety, quality improvement, ethics/professionalism, communication and team care
units.casePractice: Use a fictional case to provide a one-minute oral handoff: salient positives/negatives, differential, urgency, what is unknown, and who must evaluate.
units.assessment: Integrated case: 30% clinical reasoning, 20% domain coverage, 20% evidence/date citation, 15% safety/escalation, 15% clarity/uncertainty.

assignment.title: Integrated fictional case conference portfolio
assignment.prompt: Submit four original, fictional case analyses selected from the unit case prompts (one urgent symptom, one cross-domain case, one pediatric case, and one image/report interpretation using a lawful source link only). For each: problem representation, prioritized differential with dangerous alternatives, evidence needed, source/date citations, uncertainty statement, safe escalation/handoff, and a short oral explanation. No patient images or personal health information may be copied.
assignment.submissionNote: Do not submit real patient data or images. Constructed cases must be labeled fictional.

assessment.format: Unit retrieval quizzes and case worksheets plus a capstone oral case presentation using original fictional scenarios. Learner mastery is self-study feedback only; the course is not psychometrically validated, official ABO content, or a board-passing predictor.
assessment.masteryPlan: Suggested formative threshold: 80% on self-authored question bank after review, followed by correction of all missed rationales. This educational threshold is not an exam standard or prediction.
components: 8–10 minute oral case presentation graded to posted rubric

studyHours.note: Transparent learner workload plan, not observed clinical training: 44.1047h linked video viewing (42 unique public recordings), 43h reading and source comparison, 28h case work and assignments, 15h retrieval practice and review, 9.9h capstone preparation. Time values are a planning recommendation and are not added to verified video time or ACGME training hours.

mapping.name: Ophthalmology Residency Program
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The official directory names the Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center, ACGME as accreditor, and four years. Wilmer’s program page identifies The Johns Hopkins Hospital/Wilmer as sponsor, says selected residents rotate through eight subspecialties, describes daily 7 a.m. teaching rounds for PGY-2 and PGY-3, and reports PGY-1 and PGY-3 Bayview clinical rotations. Public pages do not supply a complete rotation schedule, case log, named eight-subspecialty rotation list, annual dated curriculum, or public resident didactic recordings; no inaccessible LMS is represented as available. The public page does not establish one unique curricular format for all entrants; ACGME allows a 48-month integrated format or a joint preliminary PGY-1 plus 36-month ophthalmology format.
