unitMap.text: Visual system foundations, examination logic and optical anatomy
coveredTopics: Visual pathways and ocular anatomy
Acuity, pupils, fields, motility, anterior segment and fundus examination concepts
Optics and imaging fundamentals; evidence and uncertainty

unitMap.text: Cornea, external disease and anterior segment
coveredTopics: Corneal anatomy/pathology; surface disease; keratitis and ulcer patterns
Conjunctival/scleral disorders; trauma, exposure, and diagnostic-test limitations

unitMap.text: Lens, cataract, aphakia and pseudophakia
coveredTopics: Lens embryology, pathology, cataract and IOLs
Aphakia, pseudophakia, capsular bag and complication reasoning

unitMap.text: Glaucoma: diagnosis, structure/function and secondary causes
coveredTopics: Glaucoma suspect and primary/secondary glaucoma; pediatric overlap
Structural-functional concordance, progression and measurement limitations
Current clinical practice cross-check against current AAO PPP

unitMap.text: Retina, vitreous, vascular and macular disease
coveredTopics: Retinal anatomy and pathology; macular/vascular/choroidal conditions
Vitreous and peripheral retinal abnormalities, retinal breaks/detachment, ocular trauma
Diabetic retinopathy, age-related and inherited disease concepts

unitMap.text: Uveitis, scleritis and masquerade reasoning
coveredTopics: Anterior, intermediate, posterior and panuveitis
Infectious/noninfectious etiologies; pediatric overlap; scleritis; masquerade syndromes

unitMap.text: Neuro-ophthalmology, pupils, fields, motility and pain
coveredTopics: Optic neuropathy, papilledema, diplopia, nystagmus and pupillary disorders
Visual fields, headache/eye pain and imaging; functional visual loss as a positive diagnosis only after appropriate assessment

unitMap.text: Oculofacial plastics, eyelids, lacrimal system and orbit
coveredTopics: Eyelid anatomy/pathology, ptosis and adnexal lesions
Orbit pathology, orbital imaging, lacrimal drainage and oculofacial principles

unitMap.text: Pediatric ophthalmology, amblyopia, strabismus and congenital disease
coveredTopics: Pediatric anterior and posterior segment, retina and glaucoma
Sensory/motor physiology, strabismus, amblyopia, nystagmus, ocular manifestations of systemic disease

unitMap.text: Refraction, optics, visual physiology and low-vision concepts
coveredTopics: Refraction and accommodation; optics; visual physiology; contact lens/refractive surgery concepts
Instrumentation, low-vision and test limitations

unitMap.text: Ocular tumors, pathology, ultrasonography and multimodal interpretation
coveredTopics: Intraocular and orbital tumors; ocular pathology; ultrasound basics
Differential diagnosis, image limitations, referral and multidisciplinary review

unitMap.text: Integrated board-style reasoning, safety, ethics and quality
coveredTopics: ABO cross-domain WQE tasks and oral case format; patient safety, diagnostic error, ethics, communication, QI, team-based care
Critical appraisal, guideline date checking, image provenance and copyright

topicGaps: The freely available recordings are archives (2020 and 2022); they are not a full current guideline course. Current clinical pathways, new evidence and local protocols need an expert date-check before use.
Public sources do not expose all Wilmer lectures or the named schedule for its eight rotation areas; none is invented or counted.
ABO blueprint lists weights but is expressly a study outline, not a comprehensive guide. The course does not duplicate proprietary board questions or official case materials.

Recorded lectures cover broad subspecialty areas but no complete, verified systematic coverage of quality improvement, ethics, contemporary evidence updates or all board tasks; use unit readings and planned source-backed microlectures.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardStatus.status: The ABO certifies physicians in ophthalmology; its current initial-certification process has a Written Qualifying Examination (WQE) and an Oral Examination after accredited residency. This is one specialty board, not separate board examinations for each ophthalmic subspecialty.
boardStatus.separateBoardExam: Yes: ABO WQE and ABO Oral Examination are separate steps within the same ophthalmology initial-certification process. No separate subspecialty board examination is represented here.
boardStatus.blueprintScope: The 2026-effective WQE outline, revised March 2025, has nine domains: Lens and Cataract 13%; Cornea, External Disease, and Anterior Segment 13%; Glaucoma 14%; Neuro-Ophthalmology 10%; Oculofacial, Plastics, and Orbit 10%; Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus 10%; Refractive Management and Optics 8%; Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors 15%; Uveitis 8%. Cross-domain aspects: presentation; diagnostic testing; management/outcomes/complications/prognosis; pathophysiology/basic science/histology/epidemiology/risk assessment. Oral exam is case-based across six areas: anterior segment; optics/visual physiology/refractive correction; pediatrics/strabismus; external eye/adnexa; neuro-ophthalmology/orbit; posterior segment. Board blueprint is not a residency syllabus or pass predictor.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Completion of this independent course does not establish medical degree, ACGME residency completion, ABO eligibility, supervised case/procedure experience, clinical competence, state licensure, board certification, or likelihood of passing. The ABO determines eligibility under its current rules. Check the ABO and ACGME directly.

officialProgrammes.name: Ophthalmology Residency Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The official directory names the Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center, ACGME as accreditor, and four years. Wilmer’s program page identifies The Johns Hopkins Hospital/Wilmer as sponsor, says selected residents rotate through eight subspecialties, describes daily 7 a.m. teaching rounds for PGY-2 and PGY-3, and reports PGY-1 and PGY-3 Bayview clinical rotations. Public pages do not supply a complete rotation schedule, case log, named eight-subspecialty rotation list, annual dated curriculum, or public resident didactic recordings; no inaccessible LMS is represented as available. The public page does not establish one unique curricular format for all entrants; ACGME allows a 48-month integrated format or a joint preliminary PGY-1 plus 36-month ophthalmology format.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Item-packet verification: this is a genuine clinical physician ophthalmology residency listed by Johns Hopkins, not an optometry residency, technician course, research-only postdoctoral post, non-physician supplement, or generic directory category. The listing names ACGME and a four-year duration. ACGME requirements currently allow the two training formats described above. No combined-programme claim is made. Johns Hopkins Hospital and Bayview are named sites under the same official residency, not separately counted institutional variants. The supplied item lists one institutional variant; no Harvard offering was added. The public curriculum is partial. ACGME requirements and ABO blueprint are separate from the local program description.
sourceCaveats: Official JHM listing identifies ACGME as accreditor and a four-year program; ACGME requirements provide alternative 48-month integrated or PGY-1 plus 36-month format. Individual entrant pathway is not inferred.
Wilmer official page says eight subspecialties but public rendered page does not identify all eight or publish detailed rotation dates; exact schedule remains unknown.
ABO WQE content outline is effective for 2026 and last updated March 2025; ABO can revise it. Oral exam public source lists case-topic areas and is not reproduced.
Clinical guidance sources are date-specific. AAO PPP pages state their materials are copyright-protected; this course links, does not reproduce.
YouTube duration metadata was collected once on 2026-10-07 from publicly listed annual playlists. Individual play availability was not tested separately; exact runtime may change with edits.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient reports new flashes and floaters. Which learning-oriented next step best reflects safe reasoning?

options.text: Reassure because flashes are never associated with retinal breaks.
Treat the symptom report as requiring prompt ophthalmic assessment for vitreoretinal pathology; a self-study vignette cannot rule out a tear.
Diagnose retinal detachment from symptoms alone.
Conclude the symptoms are migraine without an examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Symptoms are not diagnostic, but acute flashes/floaters can accompany PVD, retinal breaks or detachment. AAO guidance makes examination and risk context essential; this is an educational safety answer, not individualized triage advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional longitudinal glaucoma record shows progressive RNFL thinning with matching repeatable visual-field change despite IOP readings within a population reference range. What is the best inference?

options.text: Glaucoma is excluded by normal-range IOP.
Structure and function may provide complementary evidence; normal-tension glaucoma remains in the differential.
OCT alone proves the diagnosis and severity.
A single pressure reading establishes progression.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Current AAO PPP notes some POAG occurs with untreated IOP in the normal range and that structural and functional tests are complementary; clinical diagnosis is not made from one test or this fictional exercise.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which finding is most directly part of the ABO 2026 WQE domain-weight framework rather than a new separate ophthalmology board?

options.text: Glaucoma, 14% of content distribution
A standalone retina board examination
A separate board for uveitis
A mandatory ophthalmology physics board

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO lists glaucoma as a WQE domain with 14% weight. The ABO certifies in ophthalmology, not ophthalmic subspecialty boards.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which two types of evidence does the current POAG PPP identify as complementary for monitoring progression?

options.text: Visual fields and structural OCT imaging
Color vision and refraction only
One IOP measurement and symptom report
Ultrasound and blood pressure only

practiceQuestions.rationale: The PPP explicitly describes functional visual-field testing and structural OCT as complementary; their interpretation still requires qualified clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with diabetes has reduced central vision and imaging consistent with possible center-involved diabetic macular edema. Which statement best describes the 2024 AAO PPP at a high level?

options.text: Anti-VEGF agents are one evidence-supported treatment approach for center-involved DME with vision loss; individual treatment requires a clinician.
PRP is never used in proliferative disease.
A home photograph alone establishes all treatment decisions.
All center-involved edema requires the same immediate procedure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO PPP describes anti-VEGF efficacy for center-involved DME with vision loss and preserves individualized assessment. It also discusses PRP for PDR and possible observation in select eyes with good acuity; no single vignette chooses patient treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the safest interpretation of a fictional red eye with photophobia and contact-lens use when a brief text vignette supplies no examination?

options.text: A benign conjunctivitis diagnosis is certain.
Keep corneal infection/ulcer among urgent differentials and identify the need for direct professional examination.
Photophobia rules out corneal disease.
Recommend self-treatment from a general lecture.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Symptoms and contact-lens history can affect risk, but a vignette cannot establish cause. Corneal disease is an important differential and requires clinician assessment.

options.text: Yes, because video completion equals residency.
No; board eligibility depends on current board rules and qualifying accredited training, not an independent course.
Yes, after 36 video hours.

options.text: The curriculum includes at least 360 hours of structured basic and clinical science education during PGY-2-4, separate from this independent media tally.

title: Uveitis and Ocular Immunology Fellowship
prerequisites: Intended for advanced ophthalmology learners (ophthalmology residents/fellows/physicians); assumes medical-school-level anatomy, physiology, microbiology, immunology, pharmacology and clinical reasoning.

Prior ophthalmology training is needed to benefit fully from examination and imaging topics. The Hopkins fellowship itself expects an accredited ophthalmology residency; this independent syllabus cannot substitute for it.
No patient access, direct examination practice, procedural instruction, supervision or institutional enrollment is provided.
objectives: Localize and describe intraocular inflammation using SUN terminology while distinguishing observed signs from etiologic hypotheses.
Build a targeted infectious, immune-mediated, drug-related and masquerade differential using pretest probability and the clinical phenotype.
Explain indications and limitations of ophthalmic examination, OCT, fluorescein angiography, ultrasound, perimetry and selected laboratory/radiologic testing.
Discuss current evidence and broad safety principles for infectious and noninfectious uveitis, steroid harms, immunomodulatory therapy and systemic co-management.
Interpret clinical research classification criteria as research tools and evaluate study results, uncertainty and generalizability.
Map broad knowledge and case-reasoning objectives to ABO ophthalmology WQE/oral examination constructs and AUPO-FCC uveitis educational domains without claiming a separate uveitis board blueprint.

assignment: 12-unit formative portfolio. For every unit, create a one-page fictional-case reasoning note: concise problem representation, anatomic localization and standardized grading if provided, ranked differential with evidence and uncertainty, targeted test plan and limitations, time-critical safety flags, and a patient-centered follow-up/communication concept. Use public sources and date-check them. No real patient details or images. Global rubric: localization/problem representation 20%; evidence and differential 25%; testing and interpretation 20%; safety, urgency and uncertainty 20%; communication/citations 15%. Final synthesis: compare two plausible explanations and explain what new finding would change your reasoning.
assessment: Formative self-check questions and written assignments; 10 original educational multiple-choice questions included. No validated cut score, psychometric validation, board-question reuse, clinical competency assessment or predictor of board passing. Revise against current ABO materials and date-sensitive clinical sources.

studyHours.basis: Transparent self-study plan, not training credit: 12 units × 6 hours (72); portfolio tasks × 2 hours (24); original questions, retrieval practice and integrated synthesis (24) = 120 planned hours. Video runtime is tracked separately and not included in this planning total.

mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The current official page calls it “Ocular Immunology and Uveitis Fellowship”; it reports the program was established in 1989, participates in the Ophthalmology Fellowship Match Program, offers one year of clinical training, and an optional second research year. It gives headings for clinical operations, schedule, research, didactics/conferences/CME and evaluation, but no complete rotation schedule, lecture inventory or recorded-hour totals. Applicants should complete an accredited residency, preferably in the US. Page does not explicitly state this individual fellowship is ACGME-accredited; do not infer accreditation from the broader Hopkins directory category. Optional additional clinical research leading to an advanced degree is a research supplement, not an additional board specialty.

topicGaps: Verified video ledger: 54 unique public IUSG recordings, 105.05 hours (378176 observed seconds); this exceeds the 36-hour target by 69.05 hours. The 36-hour target is not a claim of clinical training or readiness.

The eight inherited Moran CORE candidate items retain unknown duration and are excluded from hours. Their catalog pages do not provide duration in this evidence pass; YouTube duration extraction was not verified. Their free playback also needs item-level rechecking.

The public runtime/title ledger does not expose full transcripts or prove that each concept was taught in a particular depth. Unit mappings are topic-level mappings from the public session titles and IUSG archive, not transcript-confirmed learning outcomes.

Additional source-backed learning remains useful for standardized SUN grading and documentation, targeted test selection, research-versus-clinical criteria, pediatric risk-qualified follow-up, and source-date checking. The authored scripts address these gaps but are scripts only, not video hours.
No separate uveitis board examination or uveitis-specific ABO blueprint was identified. Parent ophthalmology board mapping remains broad, not weighted or board-passing predictive.

The historical 36-item clip-plan target-minute totals (if retained by prior packet versions) never constituted rendered media or verified hours; this expansion reports only public external recordings with observed runtimes.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Ophthalmology (ABO) Written Qualifying Examination (WQE)
American Board of Ophthalmology (ABO) Oral Examination
medical.boardStatus: Uveitis/Ocular Immunology is a physician clinical fellowship subspecialty, but the official ABO public exam pages reviewed list primary ophthalmology written and oral certification examinations and no separate uveitis board examination. The uveitis fellowship is not itself an ABO certificate or distinct board exam. The program packet’s generic Johns Hopkins directory category “ACGME Accredited or Equivalent” is a directory heading, not proof that this specific fellowship is ACGME-accredited. AUPO-FCC publishes fellowship standards; current individual Hopkins AUPO-FCC status was not independently verified. No separate uveitis board eligibility is claimed.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABO certification eligibility is determined by the ABO and requires appropriate accredited medical/ophthalmology training, licensure and passing the board’s examinations. Johns Hopkins states that applicants should have completed an accredited ophthalmology residency. This self-study course provides no accredited training, case experience, supervised clinical skills, licensure, eligibility, credential or certification. ABO primary board examination content is broader than uveitis; no dedicated uveitis blueprint or standalone uveitis board exam was identified.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine — Wilmer Eye Institute
officialProgrammes.name: Ocular Immunology and Uveitis Fellowship (item packet title variant: Uveitis and Ocular Immunology Fellowship)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The current official page calls it “Ocular Immunology and Uveitis Fellowship”; it reports the program was established in 1989, participates in the Ophthalmology Fellowship Match Program, offers one year of clinical training, and an optional second research year. It gives headings for clinical operations, schedule, research, didactics/conferences/CME and evaluation, but no complete rotation schedule, lecture inventory or recorded-hour totals. Applicants should complete an accredited residency, preferably in the US. Page does not explicitly state this individual fellowship is ACGME-accredited; do not infer accreditation from the broader Hopkins directory category. Optional additional clinical research leading to an advanced degree is a research supplement, not an additional board specialty.

officialProgrammes.name: MEE Ocular Immunology and Uveitis Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exactly one clinical physician fellowship, Johns Hopkins Wilmer, preserved with official page nomenclature and packet title variant. No Harvard-affiliated variant was present in the supplied item packet; no comprehensive Harvard/Hopkins directory audit is claimed in this one-specialty task. The separate optional research year/advanced-degree research pathway is not recast as a second clinical fellowship. No non-physician or research-only category is merged.
sourceCaveats: The Hopkins page directly verifies a clinical physician fellowship with one clinical year and optional research year; public curricula are headings, not a complete formal lecture schedule. Exact Hopkins accreditation/compliance standing was not established from the public page.

The supplied packet says a Hopkins directory search category “ACGME Accredited or Equivalent”; this category is not individual programme proof. ACGME ophthalmology requirements and AUPO-FCC uveitis fellowship guidelines are distinct source types.

AUPO-FCC 2017 PDF contains fellowship standards including minimum clinical experience counts; these are standards, not evidence of current Hopkins case volumes, eligibility or learner outcomes. No actual patient/case volume is asserted for Hopkins.

ABO public pages describe WQE and oral examination for ophthalmology. No separate uveitis board exam or dedicated exam blueprint was identified; absence from reviewed page is qualified, not a claim about every credentialing entity worldwide.
YouTube public metadata extraction failed to provide candidate durations; candidate video pages remain unknown and excluded. Current playback and free access were not fully verified.

Clinical sources were checked 2026-10-07; CDC page extraction failed, so management details were intentionally not specified. Verify live CDC/guidelines and current specialist references before relying on any date-sensitive qualifier.

All questions and fictional cases are original educational content, not official ABO items or validated predictors. No real patient treatment advice, images or records are supplied. Human clinical review was not performed.

topicGaps: Verified video ledger: 54 unique public IUSG recordings, 105.05 hours (378176 observed seconds); this exceeds the 36-hour target by 69.05 hours. The 36-hour target is not a claim of clinical training or readiness.

The eight inherited Moran CORE candidate items retain unknown duration and are excluded from hours. Their catalog pages do not provide duration in this evidence pass; YouTube duration extraction was not verified. Their free playback also needs item-level rechecking.

The public runtime/title ledger does not expose full transcripts or prove that each concept was taught in a particular depth. Unit mappings are topic-level mappings from the public session titles and IUSG archive, not transcript-confirmed learning outcomes.

Additional source-backed learning remains useful for standardized SUN grading and documentation, targeted test selection, research-versus-clinical criteria, pediatric risk-qualified follow-up, and source-date checking. The authored scripts address these gaps but are scripts only, not video hours.
No separate uveitis board examination or uveitis-specific ABO blueprint was identified. Parent ophthalmology board mapping remains broad, not weighted or board-passing predictive.

The historical 36-item clip-plan target-minute totals (if retained by prior packet versions) never constituted rendered media or verified hours; this expansion reports only public external recordings with observed runtimes.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with acute unilateral painful photophobic red eye has anterior chamber cells on slit lamp. What is the most defensible first description?

options.text: Diagnose HLA-B27-associated disease from the symptom pattern alone
Classify the anatomic site and grade observed inflammation before attributing cause
Order a broad autoimmune panel before documenting the exam
Call this posterior uveitis because vision is blurred

practiceQuestions.rationale: SUN terminology separates anatomic localization and observed grading from etiologic attribution; a single phenotype does not prove an associated systemic cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best captures the intended role of SUN disease classification criteria?

options.text: They are mandatory bedside diagnostic criteria for every red eye
They prove an etiology whenever criteria are met
They are research classification criteria and should not replace individualized clinical diagnostic judgment
They replace microbiologic testing

practiceQuestions.rationale: SUN emphasizes standardized research classification; diagnostic reasoning remains clinical and must account for differential diagnosis and test context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has focal necrotizing retinitis adjacent to an old pigmented scar. What best supports considering toxoplasmic retinitis while avoiding overclaim?

options.text: A positive serum IgG alone confirms active ocular toxoplasmosis
The old scar alone proves active toxoplasmosis
Start systemic immunosuppression without excluding infection
Assess the compatible morphology, host context and evidence for alternatives; classification criteria have exclusions and are not bedside rules

practiceQuestions.rationale: SUN toxoplasmosis classification combines compatible active lesion features with evidence and exclusions. Widespread IgG seropositivity alone is not proof of active ocular infection; use current expert clinical evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner suspects ocular syphilis in a patient with uveitis. Which resource is the proper current authority for management details?

options.text: Current CDC STI treatment guidance, together with urgent clinician-led ophthalmic/infectious-disease assessment
A general NEI patient information page alone
A 2017 fellowship guideline as if it were a treatment protocol
A video clip selected by title only

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official CDC STI guideline is the management reference; this course has not transcribed treatment regimens and requires contemporaneous clinical source verification.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the most defensible laboratory testing strategy for an otherwise well patient with a low-risk isolated anterior uveitis episode?

options.text: Order every autoimmune and infectious test available in all cases
Use HLA typing alone to identify cause
Use phenotype, history and pretest probability to select tests, avoiding indiscriminate low-yield panels
Use serum ACE alone to diagnose sarcoidosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: SUN review warns that broad indiscriminate workups can generate low-specificity incidental findings; targeted evaluation follows clinical pattern and pretest probability.

practiceQuestions.stem: For children with JIA and controlled uveitis on stable therapy, which monitoring interval is strongly recommended by the cited ACR/AF guideline?

options.text: Once every 2 years
Only when the child reports pain
Only after stopping all treatment
No less frequently than every 3 months

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACR/AF guideline strongly recommends ophthalmologic monitoring no less frequently than every 3 months for controlled uveitis on stable therapy; tapering has additional, closer follow-up recommendations.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which claim is supported by the official Johns Hopkins Wilmer programme page?

options.text: A guaranteed two-year clinical fellowship for all fellows
One year clinical training, with optional second research year described
An ACGME-accredited uveitis residency
A public complete inventory of recorded lectures

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins states one year of clinical training and an optional second year devoted to research; no public complete recorded lecture inventory is provided.

practiceQuestions.stem: What statement about board examinations is best supported by the official ABO pages?

options.text: ABO describes written and oral steps for general ophthalmology certification; no separate uveitis exam is listed on its public exam page
ABO has a dedicated uveitis subspecialty board exam
Finishing this self-study course grants board eligibility
Uveitis fellowship alone grants primary ABO certification

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO public exam and eligibility pages describe primary ophthalmology certification steps, including WQE and oral exam. No standalone uveitis exam is listed. Eligibility is board-determined and training-dependent.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which imaging modality is a reasonable component of a question-driven posterior uveitis evaluation?

options.text: Order all modalities for every patient regardless of findings
Treat an OCT signal as etiologic proof
Assume an opaque-media ultrasound can identify all causes
Select OCT, fluorescein angiography, ultrasound or perimetry according to the clinical question and interpret in context

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUPO fellowship educational standards include understanding indications and interpretation for OCT, FA, ultrasound, perimetry and other studies; the appropriate test depends on context.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does a course completion certificate in this independent syllabus establish?

options.text: Supervised procedural competence
Eligibility for the ABO WQE
Only completion of this educational self-study, not accredited training, licensure, competence, or board eligibility
Certification in ocular immunology

practiceQuestions.rationale: The course is independent education; it does not substitute for supervised accredited training, licensure, eligibility or professional certification.

title: Cytopathology Fellowship
prerequisites: Learner level: postgraduate physician/pathology resident or pathologist; assumes foundational anatomic/clinical pathology, histology, microscopy, laboratory medicine, and basic evidence appraisal.
Independent self-study only. It does not supply supervised specimens, patient care, FNA practice, sign-out, feedback, or assessment by a credentialed programme.
All learners must use current reporting editions/guidelines applicable to their setting; published system revisions and management guidelines change.
objectives: Use adequacy and preparation characteristics to frame cytology interpretation.

Describe specimen allocation, quality assurance, regulatory and informatics issues relevant to cytopathology.
Practice written/practical and virtual-microscopy style reasoning without representing these exercises as official ABPath content.

assignment.title: Integrated case-based report and quality reflection
assignment.instructions: Select one linked lawfully accessible educational case/image. Do not download/rehost images. Submit an adequacy statement, concise descriptive findings, a justified standardized category, focused differential, proposed ancillary tests with material/validation limits, and a 250-word reflection on communication, quality, and uncertainty. rubric.proficient: Names sample type/preparation, adequacy limitation and key preanalytic factors.

assignment.completionThreshold: 80/100 plus correction of any safety-critical overstatement; educational progress measure only, not a validated exam or competency assessment.

unitMap.text: Orientation, specimen lifecycle, and quality
coveredTopics: Scope and specimen types
Direct smears, liquid-based preparations, cell blocks, touch imprints, core/touch preparations
Adequacy and limitations; labeling, triage, safety, quality indicators

unitMap.text: Cervical/anal cytology and Bethesda reporting
coveredTopics: Cervicovaginal and anal specimens
Specimen adequacy, NILM, squamous/glandular abnormalities
HPV ancillary tests, screening and prevention; guidelines vary and must be date-checked

unitMap.text: Thyroid FNA and Bethesda categories
coveredTopics: Nondiagnostic, benign, AUS, FN/SFN, suspicious, malignant categories
Papillary, follicular-patterned, oncocytic, medullary, thyroiditis and mimics
Clinical/imaging correlation and ancillary tests

unitMap.text: Head and neck, salivary gland, and lymph node aspirates
coveredTopics: Salivary gland Milan framework: category and risk/management associations; verify edition used
Metastatic SCC and HPV testing caveats
Lymph node patterns; flow cytometry and cell block triage

unitMap.text: Respiratory cytology and small specimens
coveredTopics: Benign/reactive, infection, primary lung tumors, metastases
Small sample triage, cell block, molecular/immuno testing and PD-L1 context
Rapid on-site evaluation: role, scope and quality checks

unitMap.text: Pancreaticobiliary and gastrointestinal cytology
coveredTopics: EUS-FNA/FNB sampling and pancreatic cyst fluid limits
Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology reporting categories and risk framing
Gastrointestinal/liver cytology differential and cell-block triage

unitMap.text: Urinary tract cytology
coveredTopics: Voided and instrumented urine; lower/upper tract distinctions
Atypical, suspicious and HGUC-oriented reporting concepts
Cellularity, degeneration, therapy effect and ancillary correlation

unitMap.text: Serous fluids, CSF, and effusions
coveredTopics: Pleural/peritoneal/pericardial fluids and CSF
International System of Reporting Serous Fluid Cytopathology concepts
Cell blocks, immunopanels, lymphoma/mesothelioma/metastatic differentials

unitMap.text: Breast, bone/soft tissue, and other site FNAs
coveredTopics: Breast FNA context and IAC Yokohama framework
Bone/soft tissue, skin, liver, adrenal, spleen and miscellaneous aspirates
Sampling strategy, morphology, cell block and ancillary workup

unitMap.text: Ancillary testing and cytomolecular diagnostics
coveredTopics: Cell blocks, immunocytochemistry, histochemistry, flow cytometry
HPV, molecular/genomic assays and predictive markers
Specimen adequacy/validation; avoiding over-interpretation

unitMap.text: Laboratory management, regulations, QA, and informatics
coveredTopics: CLIA/CAP accreditation and relevant federal requirements (refer to current regulations)
QA/QC, validation, proficiency testing, error reduction and statistics
Billing/coding, credentialing, communication, digital pathology and privacy

unitMap.text: Integrated practical diagnosis and board-style synthesis
coveredTopics: Single-best-answer reasoning across all specimen types
Virtual microscopy: locator skills, low-to-high power search, sampling caveats
Written/practical, regulations, quality and integrated case synthesis

topicGaps: The 16 pre-existing pathCast YouTube entries remain unknown-duration/unverified in this stateless review; they are retained as candidates but contribute zero hours.

No newly verified recording was mapped to Unit 1 (specimen lifecycle/quality), Unit 2 (cervical/anal Bethesda), Unit 9 (breast/bone/soft tissue), Unit 10 (ancillary/cytomolecular testing), Unit 11 (laboratory management/regulation), or Unit 12 (integrated practical/virtual microscopy). Existing reading links and plans do not replace these missing verified lecture hours.

Verified additions cover Units 3–8, but do not provide comprehensive coverage of every board-blueprint element in those units; advanced differentials, current reporting-system editions, and site-specific limits remain topic gaps.

The 2026 ABPath content specification contains a detailed list of site and laboratory domains. This course maps domains qualitatively; it does not claim a validated percentage-by-percentage blueprint concordance or full exam coverage.
Public Johns Hopkins pages do not provide its detailed rotation calendar, lecture syllabus, local case materials, or exact didactic hours.
Complete current versions of standardized systems (including Bethesda, Milan, Yokohama, Paris, PSC/WHO) may not be fully freely available; confirm the currently adopted edition and local rules.
Cervical screening recommendations vary by issuing body, age, risk history, and date; use current jurisdictional guidance.

medical.boardStatus: The official Johns Hopkins Pathology page describes a post-residency ACGME-accredited fellowship and preparation for the ABPath Added Qualification in Cytopathology examination. ABPath lists an active cytopathology subspecialty exam. This is a subspecialty certification, not a distinct primary physician specialty board exam. No Harvard-affiliated variant is in the supplied item packet; scope here is the named Johns Hopkins programme only.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABPath eligibility is governed by the Board’s current requirements and is not conferred by this independent course. ABPath describes requirements including medical education, unrestricted licensure, and current primary/subspecialty board certification for subspecialty candidates. Verify applicable pathway and current Booklet of Information directly with ABPath. ACGME fellowship participation/requirements are not equivalent to board eligibility. No guarantee of exam success.

topicGaps: The 16 pre-existing pathCast YouTube entries remain unknown-duration/unverified in this stateless review; they are retained as candidates but contribute zero hours.

No newly verified recording was mapped to Unit 1 (specimen lifecycle/quality), Unit 2 (cervical/anal Bethesda), Unit 9 (breast/bone/soft tissue), Unit 10 (ancillary/cytomolecular testing), Unit 11 (laboratory management/regulation), or Unit 12 (integrated practical/virtual microscopy). Existing reading links and plans do not replace these missing verified lecture hours.

Verified additions cover Units 3–8, but do not provide comprehensive coverage of every board-blueprint element in those units; advanced differentials, current reporting-system editions, and site-specific limits remain topic gaps.

The 2026 ABPath content specification contains a detailed list of site and laboratory domains. This course maps domains qualitatively; it does not claim a validated percentage-by-percentage blueprint concordance or full exam coverage.
Public Johns Hopkins pages do not provide its detailed rotation calendar, lecture syllabus, local case materials, or exact didactic hours.
Complete current versions of standardized systems (including Bethesda, Milan, Yokohama, Paris, PSC/WHO) may not be fully freely available; confirm the currently adopted edition and local rules.
Cervical screening recommendations vary by issuing body, age, risk history, and date; use current jurisdictional guidance.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 52-year-old has a thyroid FNA with abundant colloid and bland follicular cells, without nuclear features concerning for papillary carcinoma. Which category best communicates the findings using the six-tier Bethesda framework?

options.text: Nondiagnostic
Benign
AUS
Suspicious for malignancy

practiceQuestions.rationale: A representative aspirate showing benign follicular cells with colloid fits the benign category. Adequacy, clinical/imaging context, and local current edition criteria still matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A cervical cytology specimen is unsatisfactory because of scant cellularity. What is the best reporting principle?

options.text: Report NILM because no atypical cells are seen
Report unsatisfactory and state the reason
Report ASC-US by default
Report HSIL if HPV is positive

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Bethesda framework separately reports specimen adequacy and reason for unsatisfactory evaluation; an inadequate specimen is not a negative result.

practiceQuestions.stem: A candidate observes an epithelial abnormality interpreted as LSIL. Which statement correctly reflects the Bethesda terminology relationship?

options.text: LSIL encompasses HPV effect/mild dysplasia/CIN 1
LSIL is equivalent to invasive squamous carcinoma
LSIL excludes HPV-associated change
LSIL is a glandular category

practiceQuestions.rationale: Bethesda terminology maps LSIL to HPV/mild dysplasia/CIN 1 in cervical reporting; terminology and management must be distinguished and current guidance checked.

practiceQuestions.stem: A thyroid FNA is scant, but a few follicular groups are present. What is the most defensible initial approach?

options.text: Assume benign from any follicular cells
Assess adequacy against specimen/site criteria and report limitation/category accordingly
Diagnose follicular carcinoma based on scantness
Substitute a histologic diagnosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adequacy and category must reflect the actual sample and applicable criteria; cytology alone cannot use capsular/vascular invasion to classify follicular carcinoma.

practiceQuestions.stem: A lymph node aspirate raises a differential that includes lymphoma. Which triage step may add useful information when feasible?

options.text: Discard all fresh material before ancillary planning
Consider allocating appropriate material for flow cytometry and cell block, coordinated with the clinical question
Use HPV testing as a universal lymphoma test
Issue a definitive lymphoma subtype from morphology alone in every case

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ancillary studies can be useful, but test selection and specimen handling should be planned around differential and available material; no universal test or guaranteed definitive result.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a small lung sample workup, which statement is safest?

options.text: Use all material for one stain before assessing clinical needs
Coordinate specimen triage for morphology and clinically indicated ancillary testing while acknowledging scant-sample limitations
Cytology can always assign every molecular biomarker
A negative test in an inadequate specimen proves absence of the target

practiceQuestions.rationale: Small samples require careful allocation and explicit limitations. Test choice and validity depend on clinical context, assay validation, and specimen adequacy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pancreatic cyst aspirate has bland cytology. Which interpretation principle is appropriate?

options.text: Bland cells prove the cyst is non-neoplastic
Integrate cytology with imaging, clinical findings, and limitations of sampling; use standardized terminology where appropriate
Assign a malignant diagnosis solely from cyst location
Ignore fluid and imaging context

practiceQuestions.rationale: Cyst aspirates are subject to sampling limitations; interpretation/reporting is integrated with clinical and imaging context and the relevant reporting framework.

practiceQuestions.stem: An aspirate is submitted for suspected metastatic carcinoma, and cell block is limited. What is the best next principle?

options.text: Order a broad panel without regard to tissue exhaustion
Choose focused ancillary tests tied to a prioritized differential and preserve material where possible
Treat any positive stain as a stand-alone diagnosis
Use only a single marker to establish every primary site

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ancillary testing should answer a question, be interpreted as part of integrated morphology/context, and respect specimen adequacy and validation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description matches the ABPath Cytopathology subspecialty exam description reviewed 2026-10-07?

options.text: Only glass-slide microscopy
Written/practical and virtual microscopy sections with single-best-answer questions
A practical exam without written questions
An online course certificate

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPath describes a computer-based exam with written/practical and virtual microscopy sections, and single-best-answer questions. This does not validate any independent course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner completes this independent online course. Which claim may the course make?

options.text: Completion confers ABPath board eligibility
Completion certifies independent FNA competence
Completion is educational self-study and does not confer training, licensure, eligibility, or certification
Completion guarantees passing

practiceQuestions.rationale: Board eligibility and certification are governed by ABPath requirements, approved training, credentials, and licensure; an unaffiliated course grants none of these.

title: Dermatopathology Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced physician-level pathology or dermatology knowledge; designed for learners who have completed primary specialty training or are preparing for fellowship-level study, not patients or novice learners.
Working knowledge of skin anatomy, histology, pathology, dermatology clinicopathologic correlation, immunohistochemistry, special stains and laboratory quality assurance.
Comfort with clinical evidence appraisal and uncertainty; a virtual slide device/broadband may be necessary for some external resources.
No enrollment, patient materials, clinical access, supervision or specimen sign-out authority is provided.
objectives: Describe the specimen, site, pattern, and limitation before naming an entity.
Build and rank differential diagnoses integrating clinical distribution/history with low- and high-power morphology.
Select special stains, immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, microbiology, or molecular studies to answer a defined question and interpret their limits.
Reason across inflammatory, infectious, melanocytic, keratinocytic, adnexal, soft-tissue, vascular, lymphoid, histiocytic/deposition and special-site dermatopathology.
Communicate discordance, sampling limitations, need for consultation, and uncertainty without unsupported diagnostic certainty.
Relate course topics to the publicly available ABPath/ABD subspecialty examination outline without claiming validated exam readiness.

units.title: Specimen, report, and dermatopathology reasoning foundations
objectives: Construct a concise clinical question from site, morphology, distribution, duration, treatment, and specimen type.
Assess orientation, depth, sampling, artifact, and clinicopathologic concordance before offering a ranked differential.
units.topics: Biopsy types and limitations; clinical information; levels and sampling; nomenclature; differential-first interpretation; consultation and report communication.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology; laboratory/clinical knowledge; patient-care decision making and consultation.
units.casePractice: Use an ASDP case archive case linked by its authors; make a written problem representation from supplied clinical text before viewing images. Do not copy/rehost slides.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Clinical context 25%; specimen limitation/artifact 25%; defensible differential 30%; uncertainty/report language 20%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Inflammatory reaction patterns and vasculopathic injury
objectives: Classify dominant inflammatory pattern and distribution at low power.
Distinguish interface, perivascular/interstitial, granulomatous, and thrombotic/vasculitic patterns, retaining clinical differential.
units.topics: Pattern recognition, cell types, epidermal/dermal distribution, interface injury, eosinophils, neutrophils, vasculitis versus vasculopathy, special stain and clinical correlation.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology; related clinical/laboratory knowledge; one-best-answer visual problem solving.
units.casePractice: Compare two linked ASDP inflammatory cases with similar patterns; state morphology and limits before naming disease.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Pattern/site 35%; differential 30%; ancillary test choice 20%; limits/communication 15%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Spongiotic, psoriasiform, lichenoid, and interface dermatitis
objectives: Identify epidermal reaction patterns and discriminating histologic features.
Integrate distribution, scale, medication/exposure history, and chronicity without diagnosing from a single feature.
units.topics: Spongiosis, acanthosis, parakeratosis, lichenoid/interface dermatitis, dyskeratosis, eosinophils, infection/drug mimics, pattern overlap.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology and problem solving.
units.casePractice: Complete a pattern-to-differential matrix using one current linked ASDP case and a fictional text vignette.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Morphologic accuracy 40%; differential 30%; contextual tests/history 20%; calibrated certainty 10%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Vesiculobullous and autoimmune blistering disease
objectives: Localize a split and describe acantholysis, interface change, and inflammatory infiltrate.
Explain when direct immunofluorescence and serology complement routine histology and how specimen/site handling constrains interpretation.
units.topics: Intraepidermal versus subepidermal split; acantholysis; immunofluorescence concepts; clinical distribution; infection/drug/trauma mimics.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology, related clinical/laboratory knowledge, ancillary methods.
units.casePractice: Use linked ASDP resources and a fictional split-localization vignette; no patient material copied.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Split/primary change 35%; differential 30%; ancillary method and limitations 25%; safety/uncertainty 10%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Cutaneous infection and infection mimics
objectives: Form a differential from organism morphology and tissue response.
Choose stains, cultures, or molecular testing in context and describe false-negative/contamination limitations.
units.topics: Bacterial, fungal, viral, parasitic infection; granulomatous/suppurative patterns; special stains and clinicopathologic correlation.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology and laboratory methods.
units.casePractice: Work through linked publicly available ASDP or WebPathology teaching case. Use the original host and obey case terms.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Differential 30%; appropriate test/stain 35%; result limits 20%; clear summary 15%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Melanocytic neoplasia and melanoma work-up
objectives: Describe architectural and cytologic features and distinguish common nevus/melanoma patterns.
Explain ancillary immunohistochemical or molecular tests as adjuncts, not stand-alone arbiters, and identify sampling/correlation limits.
units.topics: Melanocytic nevi, Spitz spectrum, dysplastic nevi, melanoma patterns, regression, molecular ancillary testing, reporting concepts.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology; visual microscopy; ancillary immunohistochemical/molecular tests.
units.casePractice: Compare the differential in a text-only fictional vignette and a linked virtual slide if terms allow; avoid practice from copied images.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Architecture/cytology 35%; differential 25%; ancillary interpretation 20%; limits and communication 20%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Keratinocytic, adnexal, cystic, and epidermal tumors
objectives: Recognize differentiation and architecture in common epidermal/adnexal lesions.
Frame benign/malignant differential and select additional work-up only when clinically indicated.
units.topics: Keratinocytic proliferations; basal/squamous patterns; follicular/sebaceous/eccrine/apocrine differentiation; cysts; mimics and molecular/IHC adjuncts.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology, practical image-based interpretation.
units.casePractice: Use linked ASDP virtual slide/case resource; produce a one-paragraph differential and note the sample’s limits.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Morphology 40%; differential/risk flags 25%; ancillary choice 20%; source and caveat 15%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Cutaneous soft-tissue, neural, and vascular tumors
objectives: Classify a lesion by compartment, growth pattern, cytology, and stromal/vascular features.
Recognize when immunohistochemistry or molecular testing is needed to separate mimics and when expert consultation is appropriate.
units.topics: Cutaneous spindle-cell lesions, neural tumors, vascular neoplasms, DFSP and mimics, soft-tissue differential, staging/report implications.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology; special technical and ancillary methods; consultation.
units.casePractice: Use a dermatopathology board-review video plus an ASDP link for case comparison; no rehosting or diagnosis based solely on video examples.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Compartment/pattern 30%; differential 30%; test selection 20%; consultation/limits 20%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Granulomatous, depositional, histiocytic, and metabolic disorders
objectives: Differentiate granulomatous response types and relate distribution to plausible causes.
Recognize deposits/histiocytic patterns and select stains/tests while considering systemic and infectious differentials.
units.topics: Granuloma pattern; foreign body versus infectious/inflammatory processes; xanthogranulomatous lesions; cutaneous deposits and systemic associations; stains.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology; related clinical and laboratory knowledge.
units.casePractice: Create a differential tree for a fictional granulomatous/deposition case and compare with linked ASDP/virtual-slide teaching content.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Pattern 30%; competing causes 30%; stain/test interpretation 25%; uncertainty 15%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Cutaneous lymphoid and hematolymphoid proliferations
objectives: Describe epidermotropism, cytology, distribution, and immunophenotype as a combined evidence set.
Separate reactive infiltrates from cutaneous lymphoma cautiously and state the need for clinical, molecular, and longitudinal correlation.
units.topics: T-cell and B-cell infiltrates, pseudolymphoma, CD30+ proliferations, mycosis fungoides mimics, ancillary studies and reporting.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology; immunohistochemistry/molecular ancillary tests; patient-care/consultation.
units.casePractice: Use the ASDP peer-reviewed case archive when an item is accessible; prepare evidence table without copying images or protected content.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Morphology 30%; differential 25%; immunophenotype/context 25%; uncertainty and communication 20%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Hair, nail, mucosal, pediatric, and special-site pathology
objectives: Identify site-specific normal structures and patterns in hair/nail/mucosal biopsies.
Account for age, site, sampling, and specialized clinical history before interpreting findings.
units.topics: Alopecia pattern and level, nail unit, oral/anogenital special sites, pediatric lesions, specimen selection and pitfalls.
units.boardDomains: ABPath diagnostic dermatopathology; clinically related knowledge.
units.casePractice: Select an authentic, de-identified ASDP case that is publicly accessible and permitted for individual viewing; otherwise complete fictional written exercise.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Anatomic localization 30%; pattern 30%; clinical correlation 25%; limitations 15%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

units.title: Ancillary testing, digital microscopy, laboratory quality, and integrated unknowns
objectives: Choose IHC, histochemical, microbiologic, immunofluorescence, and molecular tests to answer a specific differential question.
Interpret results with validation, preanalytic, analytic, and postanalytic limitations; communicate discordance and escalation.
units.topics: Appropriate-use reasoning; quality assurance; digital versus glass microscopy constraints; consults; reporting; multidisciplinary correlation; exam-style image/case synthesis.
units.boardDomains: ABPath exam description: diagnostic dermatopathology, related clinical/lab knowledge, gross/microscopic diagnoses, microscopy, ancillary tests, lab management/QA, patient-care decisions and consultation.
units.casePractice: Timed original unknown set built from links to licensed/public case archives; never transcribe board questions or rehost patient material.
units.assessment: Formative written/image reasoning assignment. Rubric: Question addressed by test 25%; result interpretation 25%; specimen/QC limits 20%; integrated differential 20%; communication 10%. This is not competency assessment, board credit, or independent sign-out authorization.

assignment.title: 12-unit Clinicopathologic Reasoning Portfolio
assignment.instructions: For each unit, create a one-page differential/decision map from an original fictional text vignette or a linked, lawfully viewable ASDP educational case. Do not download, screenshot, reproduce, upload, or rehost case images, patient records or archived board material. Cite the actual host, item terms and source date. For each case state the pattern, discriminating features, differential, test purpose, limitations and conclusion wording. The capstone synthesizes an unknown across pattern, ancillary evidence and discordance. This is not clinical reporting or sign-out.

assessment.format: Formative unit case assignments, short-answer/checkpoint reflection, and 10 original multiple-choice educational questions included below.
assessment.limitations: Items are original, not validated, psychometrically calibrated, official ABPath/ABD questions, or predictive of passing. No passing score, certification or clinical competency assessment is provided.

studyHours.basis: Transparent self-study plan: 12 units x 5 hours (60), portfolio/linked case assignments 24 hours, spaced retrieval and integrated review 12 hours = 96 planned learner hours. Plan only; not measured video time, accredited credit, clinical training, or a representation of the institutional fellowship calendar.

unitMap.text: Specimen, report, and dermatopathology reasoning foundations
Inflammatory reaction patterns and vasculopathic injury
Spongiotic, psoriasiform, lichenoid, and interface dermatitis
Vesiculobullous and autoimmune blistering disease
Cutaneous infection and infection mimics
Melanocytic neoplasia and melanoma work-up
Keratinocytic, adnexal, cystic, and epidermal tumors
Cutaneous soft-tissue, neural, and vascular tumors
Granulomatous, depositional, histiocytic, and metabolic disorders
Cutaneous lymphoid and hematolymphoid proliferations
Hair, nail, mucosal, pediatric, and special-site pathology
Ancillary testing, digital microscopy, laboratory quality, and integrated unknowns

topicGaps: The unique, accessible recording ledger clears the 36-hour media floor but remains a topical inventory, not a balanced, validated curriculum or board-readiness measure. Unit 11 now has a directly timed 32:29 nail-unit clinicopathology lecture; existing alopecia media plus linked open review strengthen hair coverage. Freely accessible full-length instruction remains comparatively thin for pediatric dermatopathology, mucosal/anogenital biopsy interpretation, contemporary laboratory QA and appropriate-use workflows, digital-slide validation in dermatopathology-specific practice, and integrated ancillary-test use. The authored episodes add source-grounded teaching inputs but are scripts only, not verified video hours.

Several long-form recordings are old or have undetermined publication dates. Current high-stakes rules and practice must be checked against the dated current official ABPath/ACGME material and the relevant laboratory or clinical service protocol; runtimes do not support clinical recommendations.

Existing YouTube recording durations were observed from public metadata as described in their individual records. The newly added nail item duration was directly visible on its public watch page. Neither this audit nor page access constitutes independent audiovisual playback, content-level peer review, or assurance of continuing availability. Public access may vary by platform or geography.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact supplied item packet identifies a Johns Hopkins School of Medicine clinical Dermatopathology Fellowship. Verified official programme page plus the parallel department page establish one actual physician fellowship (not a generic directory category or non-physician supplement), with ACGME accreditation stated by Hopkins. Pathology-trained and dermatology-trained fellows have different rotation emphases inside one offering; do not treat them as distinct independent specialties. ABD/ABPath subspecialty certification is joint and a separate examination exists. The program includes research/teaching as components, not a research-only fellowship. No Harvard-affiliated distinct program was supplied or established here; no comprehensive Harvard/Johns Hopkins directory audit is claimed.
sourceCaveats: The ACGME Dermatopathology Program Requirements and FAQs PDF was fetched; its revision information states requirements/FAQs effective July 1, 2026 (with an interim revision effective February 9, 2026). ACGME standards govern accredited programs, not this self-study course.

The ABPath/ABD certification route is joint. ABD page contains historic candidate rules and describes 10-year time-limited certificates; the ABPath 2026 Booklet gives current seven-year general period for post-2019 subspecialty training. Check board-specific rules and exceptions with both boards; do not combine older ABD time limits with ABPath rules as if identical.
Johns Hopkins 2026–2027 application page uses a past application timeline; those details were not relied upon for current recruitment. The two program pages are descriptions of one offering.
No exact case counts, diagnostic volumes, board pass rates, learner outcomes, funded-seat guarantee, or eligibility beyond board/program statements are inferred. Public pages may be incomplete.
The course is not affiliated with or endorsed by Johns Hopkins, Harvard, ACGME, ABPath, ABD, ASDP or video providers. No institutional course materials are reproduced.
Clinical images have not been copied. Authentic linked case resources have item-specific access, anonymization and reuse terms. Public availability does not authorize redistribution.

The 2026 ABPath blueprint page links a 2026 exam blueprint but labels content specifications as draft general guides for 2025. Use official current board documents; no actual/proprietary board items are included.

This curriculum is educational self-study. It does not replace medical school, accredited clinical training, microscope and laboratory experience, supervision, licensure, board eligibility, certification, professional judgment or direct patient care. No diagnosis/treatment advice, unsupervised procedure, sign-out, or clinical authorization is provided. Human clinical review is not performed.

topicGaps: The unique, accessible recording ledger clears the 36-hour media floor but remains a topical inventory, not a balanced, validated curriculum or board-readiness measure. Unit 11 now has a directly timed 32:29 nail-unit clinicopathology lecture; existing alopecia media plus linked open review strengthen hair coverage. Freely accessible full-length instruction remains comparatively thin for pediatric dermatopathology, mucosal/anogenital biopsy interpretation, contemporary laboratory QA and appropriate-use workflows, digital-slide validation in dermatopathology-specific practice, and integrated ancillary-test use. The authored episodes add source-grounded teaching inputs but are scripts only, not verified video hours.

Several long-form recordings are old or have undetermined publication dates. Current high-stakes rules and practice must be checked against the dated current official ABPath/ACGME material and the relevant laboratory or clinical service protocol; runtimes do not support clinical recommendations.

Existing YouTube recording durations were observed from public metadata as described in their individual records. The newly added nail item duration was directly visible on its public watch page. Neither this audit nor page access constitutes independent audiovisual playback, content-level peer review, or assurance of continuing availability. Public access may vary by platform or geography.

practiceQuestions.stem: A skin biopsy shows a dominant spongiotic epidermal reaction with focal parakeratosis. Which is the most defensible first interpretation?

options.text: Spongiosis is a pattern; clinical distribution, exposure/medication history and other histologic features are needed to rank eczema, drug reaction, infection and mimics.
This proves allergic contact dermatitis.
This excludes fungal infection.
This alone establishes a specific drug culprit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Spongiosis is a reaction pattern, not a uniquely identifying diagnosis. Clinicopathologic correlation and targeted ancillary testing may be needed; a single feature cannot establish etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a biopsy evaluated for an autoimmune blistering disorder, routine histology shows a subepidermal split. What is the best next general diagnostic principle?

options.text: Infer one specific antibody disease from split level alone.
Integrate split level and inflammatory pattern with clinical distribution and, when appropriate, properly collected direct immunofluorescence/serologic studies.
Ignore specimen handling because DIF is unaffected by biopsy site.
Call the finding diagnostic of infection.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Split level narrows a differential but does not identify a unique disease. DIF and serology can add evidence, and specimen site/handling affect interpretability. Correlation remains necessary.

practiceQuestions.stem: A melanocytic proliferation has atypical architecture and cytology in a partial biopsy. A molecular ancillary result is reported as supportive of one entity. Which interpretation is safest?

options.text: The ancillary result independently replaces morphology and clinical correlation.
Integrate morphology, sampling, clinical context and the validated scope/limitations of the ancillary assay; document unresolved discordance.
A molecular result always rules out melanoma.
A partial biopsy cannot be interpreted at all.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ancillary methods supplement rather than automatically supersede histology. Assay validation, sampling and clinicopathologic concordance matter; discordance should be communicated and may warrant additional review.

practiceQuestions.stem: A granulomatous dermatitis is present in a fictional case with systemic symptoms. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat granulomas as synonymous with sarcoidosis.
Describe granuloma type/distribution, keep infectious, foreign-body, inflammatory and systemic causes in the differential, and select stains/cultures or other tests based on the clinical question.
Order every stain in every case without a hypothesis.
Ignore clinical history because granuloma morphology is definitive.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Granulomatous patterns have broad infectious, foreign-body, inflammatory, and systemic differentials. Test selection should address a specific question and be interpreted with its sensitivity and sampling limits.

practiceQuestions.stem: A dermal spindle-cell tumor has overlapping morphology among several entities. What does an immunohistochemical panel contribute?

options.text: A panel should be chosen to test a differential and interpreted with morphology; no marker or panel is automatically diagnostic in isolation.
A large panel can replace review of the biopsy.
A single positive stain always establishes benign behavior.
IHC cannot contribute to dermatopathology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPath exam scope explicitly includes ancillary immunohistochemical and molecular methods, but interpretation must be integrated with morphologic and clinical evidence and limitations.

practiceQuestions.stem: A lymphoid infiltrate has epidermotropism and an abnormal-looking immunophenotype in one biopsy. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: One isolated biopsy always proves cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
Integrate histology, immunophenotype, clinical distribution/history, and, where relevant, longitudinal or molecular data; communicate the differential and limitations.
Immunophenotype is irrelevant.
A reactive mimic is impossible once epidermotropism is seen.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reactive and neoplastic processes may overlap. The interpretation relies on integrated evidence; a single feature or assay should not be overcalled.

practiceQuestions.stem: A biopsy from a deep dermal nodule is transected at the base. The morphology suggests a lesion whose deepest extent affects classification. What should the report reasoning emphasize?

options.text: State the limitation and avoid unsupported claims about full depth/extent; recommend correlation or additional sampling when clinically warranted.
Assume the lesion is confined to the dermis.
Treat transection as proof of malignancy.
Ignore the specimen limitation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Sampling and orientation impose limits. Reports should not make claims beyond the specimen and should communicate when additional evaluation is necessary.

practiceQuestions.stem: A virtual slide appears to show a subtle feature, but image resolution/scan quality is poor and the clinical picture is discordant. What is the best action in a learning scenario?

options.text: Treat digital image as unquestionable ground truth.
State technical limits, re-evaluate source slide/scan quality where appropriate, obtain clinical context and seek qualified review rather than force a diagnosis.
Ignore discordant clinical information.
Use a generated image as confirmatory evidence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Digital pathology can be useful but has technical and interpretive limitations described in the literature. Clinical discordance and poor image quality call for caution and expert review.

practiceQuestions.stem: A suspected cutaneous infection shows suppurative inflammation, but the first special stain is negative. Which statement is most defensible?

options.text: A negative stain always excludes infection.
Interpret the negative result in light of organism burden, sampling, stain sensitivity and the clinical question; consider additional studies if warranted.
The finding establishes a sterile inflammatory disease.
No additional work-up can ever add information.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Negative ancillary testing does not guarantee absence of organisms. Sensitivity and sampling matter, and further tests should be chosen in context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately characterizes the ABPath dermatopathology examination and its relationship to course completion?

options.text: It is a one-day subspecialty examination with written/practical and virtual microscopy sections; course completion does not confer eligibility.
It is a general dermatology residency final exam.
Any online course completion grants board eligibility.
No separate subspecialty exam exists.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPath describes a one-day computer-based dermatopathology subspecialty exam with written/practical and virtual microscopy sections. Board eligibility requires primary certification and prescribed accredited training; self-study is not eligibility.

assignment.title: GU specimen-to-report capstone (constructed cases only)
assignment.prompt: Prepare three original educational case synopses—one prostate biopsy, one TURBT/upper-tract sample, and one renal or testicular resection—using no patient records or downloaded images. For each: summarize morphology in 3–5 observations, rank a differential, justify any proposed ancillary test and its limits, map data to the relevant current CAP protocol, state missing material and uncertainty, and draft a concise educational report. Cite authoritative sources. Optionally discuss a real de-identified case only within its original host and permission conditions; do not upload patient material.
assignment.passCriteria: Practice threshold 80/100 for course progression only; not validated, board-predictive, or clinical credentialing.

assessment.format: Unit retrieval questions, case differential worksheets, oral-style written conference summary, and final capstone.
assessment.masteryRule: Self-study formative standard only; no validated passing score, no exam simulation claim, no guarantee of board performance.

unitMap.text: Diagnostic workflow, specimen handling, and safe reporting
coveredTopics: Specimen identity/orientation, biopsy/resection grossing concepts, blocks/levels, consult comparison, QA, critical communication, synoptic reporting.

unitMap.text: Prostate: benign mimics, precursor lesions, and small atypical foci
coveredTopics: Atrophy, adenosis, crowded glands, PIN, atypical small acinar proliferation, inflammation, basal-cell markers, AMACR caveats.

unitMap.text: Prostate adenocarcinoma grading and biopsy reporting
coveredTopics: Needle cores, grade heterogeneity, patterns 3–5, Grade Groups, cribriform/intraductal carcinoma, targeted/systematic sampling, structured reporting.

unitMap.text: Prostatectomy and difficult prostate tumors
coveredTopics: Orientation, mapping, margins, seminal vesicles, treatment effect, ductal/neuroendocrine and stromal mimics; use CAP protocol.

unitMap.text: Bladder and upper tract: noninvasive disease
coveredTopics: Papilloma/PUNLMP/low- and high-grade papillary UC, CIS, lamina propria, muscularis propria, artifact, upper tract.

unitMap.text: Invasive urothelial carcinoma and divergent differentiation
coveredTopics: Muscle invasion, variant histology, glandular/squamous differentiation, neuroendocrine, IHC/molecular classification, CAP reporting.

unitMap.text: Renal epithelial tumors: morphology-first classification
coveredTopics: WHO 5th edition taxonomy, clear cell, papillary, chromophobe, oncocytic, collecting-duct, molecularly defined and emerging entities.

unitMap.text: Renal tumor reporting and diagnostic problem-solving
coveredTopics: Tumor size/site/extent, grade where applicable, necrosis, margins, nodes, stage elements, hereditary/molecular clues, biopsy limits.

unitMap.text: Testis, paratestis, and germ-cell neoplasia
coveredTopics: Seminoma, embryonal carcinoma, yolk-sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, mixed tumors, GCNIS, sex-cord stromal tumors.

unitMap.text: Penis, urethra, and uncommon male genital lesions
coveredTopics: Penile SCC pathways, urethral tumors, inflammatory/reactive mimics, adnexal/paratesticular lesions, protocol mapping.

unitMap.text: Immunohistochemistry, molecular diagnostics, and differential discipline
coveredTopics: Marker selection, controls, pattern interpretation, molecularly defined renal entities, prostate/breast/colon mimics, digital pathology/AI caveats.

unitMap.text: Consultation, consensus, tumor board, QA, scholarship
coveredTopics: Outside consult comparison, consensus, frozen section correlation, CAP protocols, tumor board, research question framing, critical appraisal.

topicGaps: Verified free public recordings total 18:00:02 (18.0006 rounded hours), leaving 17:59:58 (17.9994 rounded hours) below the 36-hour video floor; no target minutes or authored scripts are counted as recorded hours.

Coverage improved for prostate intraductal carcinoma/biology, bladder and urothelial subtype classification, renal tumor taxonomy and oncocytic differentials, testicular germ-cell and non-germ-cell topics, and GU staging. Public videos remain selected talks, not a complete course.

Penile and urethral lesions, broad benign/inflammatory differential diagnosis, specimen processing/grossing, complete prostatectomy reporting, and systematic consultation/QA skills still lack sufficient verified public recorded instruction.

Existing UW prostate biology video MED128-UW-PROSTATE-BIOLOGY remains uncounted because its exact runtime and playback evidence were not verified. CAP online CME/module access and runtime remain unverified and uncounted.

Authored scripts and originalClipPlan target minutes are production inputs only; they are neither rendered recordings nor verified hours. Completing the remaining video target is feasible as an original production plan, but no recording or upload is available at this check.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One physician clinical fellowship, with institutional metadata variants preserved rather than deduplicated away. It is not a standalone residency or combined training program. The official department page explicitly labels it a clinical fellowship combining clinical and research experience; research is integral within that fellowship, not a separate non-physician track. The public Johns Hopkins Medicine listing calls it non-standard. No separate GU board examination was found in the current ABPath list. No Harvard variant identified in this supplied item; this assignment is Johns Hopkins only.
sourceCaveats: Official source pages are public descriptions, not complete institutional course syllabi. Program descriptions differ on consult volume (>20/day versus >45/day); kept as source-specific claims only.
