medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional prostate core: small crowded glands resemble carcinoma, but identical glands elsewhere retain a basal layer; cytology is uniform and no convincing infiltrative pattern is present. Best next interpretive principle?

options.text: Call adenocarcinoma because any basal-cell loss is diagnostic
Integrate architecture/cytology and treat basal markers as supportive, not standalone
Assign Grade Group 1 based only on gland size
Use AMACR positivity alone to call cancer

practiceQuestions.rationale: A focal absent basal layer does not settle a diagnosis; morphologic comparison and a context-aware interpretation are essential. Immunostains are adjuncts, and indeterminate small foci should not be upgraded by one marker.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional prostate adenocarcinoma core has predominant Gleason pattern 3 and a smaller pattern 4 component. What paired reporting framework is appropriate in contemporary practice?

options.text: Gleason score and corresponding ISUP Grade Group
Only an informal low/intermediate/high label
WHO grade only
No grade on biopsy

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ISUP consensus addresses contemporary Gleason pattern reporting and Grade Groups; use the current protocol and institutionally accepted reporting conventions. The exercise omits a numeric fraction deliberately.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about prostate grading recommendations is accurate?

options.text: Invasive cribriform carcinoma and intraductal carcinoma are irrelevant to reporting
The 2019 ISUP consensus specifically addressed reporting invasive cribriform and intraductal carcinoma
Cribriform pattern proves a germline syndrome
A single immunostain determines Grade Group

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ISUP 2019 consensus addressed reporting of invasive cribriform carcinoma and incorporation of intraductal carcinoma into grading discussions; apply current complete guidance rather than inferring inherited status from morphology.

practiceQuestions.stem: A small bladder biopsy shows a papillary urothelial lesion with inward growth. Which morphologic distinction is central before labeling invasion?

options.text: Any inverted growth equals stromal invasion
Separate non-destructive inverted growth from destructive stromal invasion
A papillary lesion cannot invade
Only p53 stain defines invasion

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO-oriented review emphasizes distinguishing inverted growth pattern from true destructive stromal invasion; assess architecture, stromal response, and sampling context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A TURBT specimen has no muscularis propria identified. What is the best report-level action?

options.text: Assume muscle invasion is absent
State the sampling limitation; do not infer a negative muscle assessment
Assign pT2 if the tumor is high grade
Substitute imaging stage for histology

practiceQuestions.rationale: An absent muscle layer limits evaluation of muscularis propria invasion; report adequacy/limitation clearly and avoid inventing a pathologic stage.

practiceQuestions.stem: A renal epithelial tumor with oncocytic cytoplasm has morphology not comfortably classifiable as a common entity. Best next step?

options.text: Force it into chromophobe RCC from cytoplasm alone
Use WHO 5th-edition taxonomy and a morphology-led differential, then select focused confirmatory tests
Diagnose benign oncocytoma based on imaging only
Assume a new entity is established from one stain

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO 5th edition includes conventional groups, molecularly defined categories and emerging entities; integrate morphology with targeted immunohistochemical/molecular evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is a correct broad testicular germ-cell classification concept from WHO 5th edition?

options.text: All germ-cell tumors derive from GCNIS
Most germ-cell tumors are divided into GCNIS-related and non-GCNIS-related families
GCNIS is a stromal tumor
Seminoma is a sex-cord stromal tumor

practiceQuestions.rationale: The WHO introduction retains a major division between tumors derived from GCNIS and those unrelated to it; seminoma is placed within the germinoma family.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional renal tumor has a morphology suggesting a molecularly defined RCC entity. How should a diagnostic workup be framed?

options.text: Choose an extensive panel without a differential
State the differential and use a focused IHC/molecular test strategy to resolve it
Treat one positive stain as a complete independent diagnosis
Skip clinicopathologic correlation

practiceQuestions.rationale: Renal classification includes molecularly defined entities, but testing is selected to answer a morphology-based differential and interpreted in context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which item is an official separate ABPath subspecialty certificate listed on the ABPath exam page?

options.text: Genitourinary pathology
Renal cell pathology
None of these listed as a distinct GU-specific certificate
Bladder pathology

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPath’s official subspecialty certificate list does not include GU, renal-cell, or bladder pathology. ABPath does have primary certification examinations; this one-year Hopkins GU fellowship is listed as non-standard, not a separate board exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hypothetical tumor board slide deck includes a public digital slide from a teaching repository. What is the sound reuse practice?

options.text: Download and rehost any free-to-view slide
Use the repository link/viewer, verify de-identification and case-level permission, and honor terms
Copy patient-linked records into slides
Assume open web access grants commercial reuse

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free viewing does not grant permission to reproduce; use de-identified authentic cases and respect item-level licenses and repository terms.

title: Hematopathology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent self-study curriculum; not training)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Graduate-level pathology knowledge; intended for pathology residents/fellows/pathologists, not for unsupervised clinical practice.
Foundational hematology, histology, immunology, clinical laboratory methods and basic molecular genetics.
Learners should be able to read a CBC/differential, basic peripheral smear descriptions and introductory immunophenotype results.
The Hopkins fellowship itself has formal physician-training and board-status prerequisites; this open course has no admissions, medical-school prerequisite verification, or clinical authority.
objectives: Integrate clinical context, specimen adequacy, blood/marrow/tissue morphology and ancillary testing in a reasoned educational report.
Compare hematolymphoid differential diagnoses across major published ABPath content domains.
Use current WHO-HAEM5 and 2022 ICC classification material with date-aware terminology.
Explain limitations of flow, immunohistochemistry, cytogenetics and molecular results.
Practice clear, safe consult communication and laboratory quality reasoning.
Identify board examination format and accurately separate self-study from supervised training/eligibility.

units.title: Specimen-first hematopathology: blood, marrow, nodes and ancillary test integration
objectives: Build a repeatable preanalytic-to-report workflow for blood, marrow, lymph node and body-fluid specimens.
Relate marrow cellularity, lineage maturation and architecture to clinical and laboratory context.
Explain when flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, cytogenetics and molecular testing add evidence rather than substitute for morphology.
topics: Specimen adequacy and triage; aspirate/biopsy correlation; peripheral smear and body fluids; immunophenotype; test limitations; integrated narrative reports
boardDomains: Blood, bone marrow, and related disorders
Patient care decision making and consultation
units.casePractice: For the explicitly fictional marrow vignette, list data needed, adequacy caveats, differential and next discriminating test; do not infer diagnosis from one marker.
units.assessment: Submit a one-page integrated report with specimen, relevant data, morphology, ancillary result interpretation, differential, limitations and concise consult communication. Rubric: 20% specimen/context; 25% morphology; 20% test integration; 20% differential/uncertainty; 15% clear report.

units.title: Myeloid neoplasms: MPN, MDS, MDS/MPN and eosinophilic entities
objectives: Organize cytopenia/cytosis evaluation around clinical history, blood/marrow morphology and exclusion of mimics.
Compare morphologic and molecular/cytogenetic evidence for myeloid categories using WHO-HAEM5 and ICC, noting differences.
Recognize when data support a defined entity versus a descriptive provisional report.
topics: MPN patterns and driver testing; MDS and dysplasia; overlap neoplasms; eosinophilia-associated rearrangements; reactive mimics; classification comparison
boardDomains: Blood, bone marrow, and related disorders
units.casePractice: Use a fictional persistent cytosis scenario to separate reactive causes from a clonal work-up; state what evidence is not yet available.
units.assessment: Create a comparative decision tree with morphology, exclusionary criteria, molecular testing and version-sensitive WHO/ICC terminology; grade on accurate criteria (40%), cautious integration (30%), and traceable sources (30%).

units.title: Acute leukemias and precursor neoplasms
objectives: Integrate blood/marrow morphology, lineage-defining immunophenotype and genetic findings in acute leukemia classification.
Distinguish acute leukemia classification from a nonspecific blast-count impression.
Explain role and limits of measurable residual disease testing and urgent communication.
topics: AML classification; lineage assignment; mixed phenotype differential; flow cytometry; defining genetic alterations; MRD; critical-value communication
boardDomains: Blood, bone marrow, and related disorders
Patient care decision making and consultation
units.casePractice: Fictional blast-rich marrow: produce a prioritized test/information checklist before choosing a final category; include a time-sensitive preliminary call.
units.assessment: Short oral-style diagnostic defense: 5-minute case presentation and written contingency statement; rubric weighs lineage evidence (35%), genetic integration (25%), uncertainty (20%) and communication (20%).

units.title: Non-neoplastic marrow, cytopenias and systemic disease
objectives: Construct a differential for pancytopenia that includes marrow failure, infection, nutrition, drugs/toxins, immune and infiltrative causes.
Compare aplastic anemia and PNH concepts with clonal myeloid mimics without overcalling clonality.
Interpret marrow findings in systemic disease and articulate when clinical correlation is necessary.
topics: Aplastic anemia, PNH, pure red-cell aplasia, agranulocytosis; congenital marrow failure; systemic infection/metabolic/drug effects; marrow cellularity and fibrosis
boardDomains: Blood, bone marrow, and related disorders
units.casePractice: Use fictional pancytopenia and medication/infection histories to rank reactive versus clonal mechanisms and identify missing reticulocyte, smear and clinical data.
units.assessment: Differential matrix with at least four mechanisms; rubric: completeness 30%, evidence matching 30%, safety/uncertainty 25%, clarity 15%.

units.title: Reactive lymphoid proliferations, methodology and diagnostic safeguards
objectives: Apply pattern-based lymph-node assessment before assigning lymphoma.
Select a focused ancillary panel that tests a differential and avoid interpreting isolated positive markers as a diagnosis.
Document tissue limitations and distinguish reactive mimics from clonal neoplasia.

boardDomains: Patient care decision making and consultation
units.casePractice: Fictional lymph-node scenario with a reactive-pattern differential: propose only the next tests that discriminate between stated alternatives.
units.assessment: Submit an IHC/flow ordering rationale; rubric 35% pattern interpretation, 30% test selection, 20% limitations, 15% resource stewardship.

units.title: Mature B-cell lymphomas: small B-cell and aggressive entities
objectives: Use morphology, distribution, immunophenotype and genetics together to distinguish common mature B-cell neoplasms.
Compare DLBCL/high-grade B-cell differential categories without conflating rearrangement results or prognostic categories.
Recognize the need to align terminology with both ICC and WHO-HAEM5.
topics: CLL/SLL; follicular, mantle, marginal-zone, lymphoplasmacytic; Burkitt; DLBCL; high-grade B-cell; primary mediastinal; differential and pitfalls

units.title: Hodgkin, T-cell and NK-cell neoplasms

units.title: Immune deficiency, EBV-associated proliferations and post-transplant lymphoproliferation
objectives: Incorporate immune status, transplant/iatrogenic context, viral studies and morphology in classification.

topics: Immune deficiency/dysregulation framework; EBV; HHV8-associated disorders; PTLD spectrum; differential with de novo lymphoma; clinical context
boardDomains: Patient care decision making and consultation
units.casePractice: Fictional transplant-associated lesion: report the known context, histologic pattern and viral evidence separately; avoid treating the setting as a diagnosis.
units.assessment: Short integrated case report; rubric: 30% context, 30% classification, 20% test interpretation, 20% caveats/communication.

units.title: Plasma-cell neoplasms and related disorders
objectives: Distinguish plasma-cell neoplasm assessment from incidental monoclonal protein alone.
Integrate marrow morphology, immunophenotype, light-chain restriction and cytogenetic/molecular findings.
Recognize the board domain overlap with erythrocyte/other clinical laboratory findings and consult appropriately.
topics: MGUS and plasma-cell myeloma concepts; plasmacytoma; plasma-cell leukemia; amyloid-related marrow work-up; differential and sampling limitations
boardDomains: Blood, bone marrow, and related disorders
Patient care decision making and consultation
units.casePractice: Fictional marrow submitted for paraproteinemia: distinguish observed plasma-cell findings from clinical diagnostic criteria not provided in the case.
units.assessment: Draft a bounded interpretive comment with required clinical correlation; rubric 30% evidence, 25% differential, 25% limitations, 20% language.

units.title: Histiocytic and dendritic-cell disorders
objectives: Recognize major histiocytic/dendritic categories and build a lineage-directed differential.
Interpret immunophenotype and MAPK-pathway findings as supportive but not individually entity-specific.
Identify when clinical, radiologic or molecular correlation remains essential.
topics: Langerhans cell histiocytosis; Rosai-Dorfman; Erdheim-Chester; histiocytic/dendritic neoplasms; HLH overview; mimics and molecular limits
boardDomains: Patient care decision making and consultation
units.casePractice: Fictional histiocytic lesion with an isolated molecular variant: write a differential and specify what does not follow from that result alone.
units.assessment: Differential map graded for lineage, marker specificity, integration and explicitly stated uncertainty (25% each).

units.title: Spleen, peripheral blood, erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets and hemostasis
objectives: Relate splenic architecture/function to common benign and neoplastic patterns.
Organize the board-relevant differential of RBC, WBC, platelet and coagulation abnormalities using CBC/smear and laboratory methods.
Identify gaps in video resources and use current primary references rather than extrapolating from lymphoid lectures.
topics: Splenic architecture and lesions; blood morphology; anemia/hemolysis and leukocyte/platelet disorders; coagulation method/interpretation; normal variants and artifacts
boardDomains: Blood, bone marrow, and related disorders
units.casePractice: Fictional smear/lab vignette: distinguish an analyzer flag from confirmed morphology and state what manual review/clinical data are required.
units.assessment: Structured laboratory interpretation worksheet; rubric 30% method/QC, 30% differential, 25% limitations, 15% communication.

units.title: Cytogenetics, molecular diagnostics, flow, quality, consultation and exam integration
objectives: Describe complementary strengths and failure modes of flow cytometry, IHC, cytogenetics and sequencing.
Apply specimen triage, validation/QC and patient-safety escalation to a fictional referral case.
Practice the exam’s written/practical/virtual-microscopy style of one-best-answer reasoning without representing the questions as official.
topics: Test methodology and analytic validity; integrated diagnosis; lab quality assurance; consult communication; multiple-choice and virtual-slide reasoning; classification date checks
boardDomains: Patient care decision making and consultation
All published ABPath domains in integrative practice
units.casePractice: Complete a fictional referral exercise with QC flags, test limitations, a preliminary consult message and a final integrated report.
units.assessment: Capstone case portfolio and 10-question self-check; rubric: accuracy 30%, methods integration 25%, safety/quality 20%, uncertainty/consultation 15%, citations 10%.

assignment.title: Fictional integrated hematopathology consult portfolio
deliverables: Write an 800–1,200-word integrated educational report for a fictional marrow/nodal referral chosen from the unit prompts.
Attach a differential table mapping findings to competing categories and identify which evidence is missing.
Add a 1-page assay-selection/quality note, a 150-word preliminary consult message and a 5-source version-aware bibliography.
Complete original formative questions and reflect on two uncertain decisions. No real patient data, images or copied board questions.

rubric.criterion: Specimen adequacy, context and accurate morphologic description
Integrated interpretation of ancillary methods and assay limits
Differential diagnosis and current classification terminology
Uncertainty, patient-safety communication and appropriate consultation caveats
Evidence quality, citations and ethical/licensing practice

assignment.limitations: Fictional teaching only, not a validated assessment, clinical report, sign-out exercise or predictor of board performance.

assessment.method: Low-stakes unit retrieval quizzes, source comparison, fictional case write-ups, and final portfolio graded with published rubric; 10 original multiple-choice items included. Learners should check responses against cited sources.
assessment.threshold: A suggested formative target is 80% on self-check items and rubric score ≥75/100 after revision. This arbitrary course completion target is not validated against ABPath outcomes and does not predict board passing.
assessment.limitations: No official exam items, protected slides or validated predictor. No clinical competency, procedure, accreditation, certification or licensure assessment.

studyHours.plan: Approximately 120–160 hours of learner time, self-paced over 12–16 weeks: about 22 hours observed external video, 50–65 hours reading, 25–35 hours case practice and retrieval, and 20–38 hours assignments/review. This is a transparent study plan, not clinical training or a minimum effective dose; change as needed.
studyHours.basis: Observed video hours come only from the deduplicated ledger. Other hours are learner planning estimates, not media duration or clinical case exposure.

mapping.name: Hematopathology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official division page: 1-year ACGME-accredited diagnostic fellowship. Lists rotations (7 months diagnostic hematopathology; 1 month each hematology/coagulation, molecular/genetic pathology, cytogenetics, laboratory management and diagnostic lymph-node pathology at NIH/NCI), weekly multidisciplinary conferences and educational resources. Institutional rotation/case service is not replicated or counted as this course’s video hours; page says information current May 28, 2025.

mapping.name: Hematopathology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official MGB programme describes a single integrated clinical fellowship with approximately two-thirds of rotations at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and one-third at Massachusetts General Hospital, plus a Boston Children’s Hospital pediatric hematopathology rotation. Includes consult, marrow, lymph-node, coagulation, flow/lab hematology, molecular/cytogenetics, weekly didactics/cases and research/QA option. This is one MGB program with shared sites, not separate MGH and BWH tracks. Entry requirements include medical-school/ECFMG status, board eligibility/certification or Canadian AP pathway and Massachusetts license; MGB residents may apply after at least two years of training as specified on its page.

unitMap.text: Cytogenetics, molecular diagnostics, flow, quality, consultation and exam integration
coveredTopics: Test methodology and analytic validity; integrated diagnosis; lab quality assurance; consult communication; multiple-choice and virtual-slide reasoning; classification date checks

topicGaps: Verified free, unique external playback currently totals 23.96444444 hours of observed duration, leaving 12.03555556 hours below the 36-hour target. Authored scripts and planned productions do not count toward this total.

Most under-served blueprint areas: non-neoplastic RBC/hemoglobinopathy morphology and interpretation; benign leukocyte, platelet and infectious blood disorders; hemostasis/thrombosis; body-fluid specimens; lab management/quality and consult; broad flow/cytogenetic/molecular methods; pediatric-context differential; and current comprehensive classification crosswalks.

Only short new direct recordings were publicly accessible: 18:44 PMF case tutorial and 19:34 introductory flow recording. A 1:24:17 ARUP AML MRD lecture strengthens AML methods coverage but does not replace a broad acute leukemia syllabus.

The 2026 ABPath blueprint assigns hemostasis/thrombosis 11% of written/practical questions plus 4% of virtual microscopy, and non-neoplastic RBC disorders 9% plus 7%; no dedicated counted long-form recording was located in the open ledger for those complete domains.

SH lectures teach useful patterns but some predate ICC 2022/WHO-HAEM5. The public SH PMF tutorial is similarly a case tutorial, not the definitive current criterion source; classification must be checked against the current ICC/WHO material.

Free ISLH archived sessions were identified but are explicitly member-only. ASH Hematology Review Series recordings require participant access. NIH Great Teachers hemostasis event remained uncounted because direct runtime evidence was unavailable. These are real source gaps, not permission to bypass access controls.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: No eligibility is conferred here. practiceQuestions.stem: An adequate marrow biopsy shows markedly increased cellularity and lineage expansion, with persistent thrombocytosis. Which diagnostic approach is most defensible before naming a specific MPN?

options.text: Use the platelet count alone to classify essential thrombocythemia.
Integrate marrow morphology, clinical data, exclusion of competing entities and relevant molecular/cytogenetic findings.
Assign primary myelofibrosis based only on cellularity.
Order broad sequencing and let any detected variant determine the diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MPN classification relies on integrated morphologic and clinical criteria with appropriately interpreted molecular/cytogenetic evidence; no single count or variant substitutes for the complete criteria.

practiceQuestions.stem: A lymph node displays a polymorphous reactive pattern with scattered immunoblasts. What is the best next principle?

options.text: Declare lymphoma based on immunoblasts.
Use architecture and clinical context to frame a differential, then select ancillary studies that discriminate among stated alternatives.
Order every available stain without a hypothesis.
Assume EBV positivity, if found, proves a specific lymphoma.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reactive and neoplastic patterns overlap. A morphology- and context-led differential with targeted ancillary studies is safer than a single-cell or single-marker conclusion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has marrow blasts and an aberrant flow phenotype. Which report statement is strongest while genetics are pending?

options.text: The flow phenotype alone establishes the final genetic AML subtype.
Report preliminary findings and lineage evidence, describe pending studies and communicate critical information promptly.
Do not communicate until the final integrated report is signed.
Infer a named genetic alteration from immunophenotype.

practiceQuestions.rationale: An integrated diagnosis requires correlation among morphology, phenotype and genetic data. A preliminary report can communicate what is known and what remains pending; ACGME requires diagnostic competence and patient-care consultation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about ABPath hematopathology certification is accurate?

options.text: No separate hematopathology examination exists.
ABPath describes a hematopathology subspecialty examination with written/practical and virtual microscopy sections.
Passing an online self-study course confers eligibility.
The exam is only a glass-slide practical.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPath describes a one-day computer-based exam with written/practical and virtual microscopy sections. Eligibility is separately governed by current board policies and is not granted by this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A post-transplant lymphoid lesion is identified in a fictional case. What must not be assumed?

options.text: Transplant history is important contextual information.
Histology and viral testing may inform classification.
The transplant setting alone identifies the specific lymphoma entity.
Immune status should be available to the interpreting team.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The transplant setting is clinically relevant but does not replace morphologic and ancillary evaluation; immunodeficiency-related proliferations span overlapping patterns and categories.

practiceQuestions.stem: A flow cytometry tube has low viability and an unexpectedly sparse event count. What is the best laboratory response?

options.text: Ignore quality flags if a clonal-looking subset is present.
Assess specimen adequacy and assay limitations, correlate with morphology/other data, and qualify or repeat testing if appropriate.
Use the event count alone to exclude disease.
Convert the preliminary finding into a definitive lymphoma diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Methodology and interpretation include analytic limitations and specimen adequacy. ACGME requires integrated use of diagnostic studies, quality practice and narrative reports.

practiceQuestions.stem: A marrow shows a small clonal plasma-cell population in a fictional case. Which conclusion is appropriate from this information alone?

options.text: The patient necessarily has symptomatic myeloma.
Clonality by itself is insufficient; interpret marrow findings with clinical diagnostic criteria and relevant studies.
The sample proves amyloidosis.
The finding is always benign.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A small clonal population cannot alone establish a clinical plasma-cell disorder category or its clinical significance; correlation with the full criteria and work-up is required.

options.text: Download and republish the image because it is viewable.
Link learners to the original page and comply with ASH terms; obtain permission before posting/copying/rehosting.
Remove the watermark and share in a public deck.
Assume free viewing means a Creative Commons license.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASH retains copyright. Its terms allow specified non-commercial personal viewing and limited classroom reproduction for accredited institutions, but prohibit public posting/network redistribution without permission. This independent course should link, not copy.

level: ACGME-accredited clinical laboratory fellowship; doctoral-level track open to qualified MD/DO and PhD trainees (not physician-only)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.intendedLearner: Advanced graduate-level self-study for genetics/genomics laboratory trainees, clinical laboratory scientists, pathologists, geneticists and physicians seeking conceptual board-blueprint preparation.
prerequisites.priorKnowledge: Molecular biology, basic genetics, cell biology, statistics, sequencing terminology and familiarity with diagnostic laboratory workflows.
prerequisites.notEligibility: No degree, enrollment, supervised case experience or board eligibility results from this course. ABMGG’s pathway is an accredited postdoctoral lab fellowship route for qualified MD/DO/PhD; confirm credential and eligibility rules with ABMGG.

objectives: Map the five published ABMGG LGG exam domains to study materials and interpret their approximate weighting.
Select a cytogenomic/molecular assay against clinical question, specimen, variant class and validated limits.
Critically classify sequence and constitutional CNV evidence with current ACMG/AMP and ClinGen guidance.
Integrate somatic testing, quality management, nomenclature, consent, privacy and report limitations.
Distinguish variant classification, individual causality, clinical actionability, accreditation requirements and board eligibility.
Explain why an independent online curriculum does not confer hands-on competence, training credit, licensure or certification.

units.title: Genome architecture, chromosomes and cell division
objectives: Relate chromatin organization, gene structure, cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis to observed genetic test findings.

Use current ISCN 2024 conventions as an aid to communicate findings, not as a substitute for the licensed nomenclature standard.
topics: Genome organization, chromatin packaging, centromeres/telomeres, nucleolar organizer regions

units.assessment: Draw a one-page segregation/meiosis mechanism map for three fictional chromosome findings; mark unresolvable mechanisms.

units.title: Chromosomal disease mechanisms and constitutional cytogenetics
objectives: Recognize common numerical and structural chromosome changes and explain plausible mechanisms.
Separate mosaicism from pseudomosaicism and identify the limits of cell-count evidence.
Choose a confirmatory method based on the question, specimen and suspected aberration.
topics: Aneuploidy/polyploidy, structural rearrangements, balanced/unbalanced events, rings, markers, recombination
Constitutional karyotype, cell culture, banding, microscopy and specimen limitations
Mosaicism, maternal-cell contamination and prenatal specimen interpretation
units.casePractice: Compare publicly curated constitutional copy-number interpretations in ClinGen; treat public variant records as reference evidence, not whole clinical case files.
units.assessment: For three fictional referral questions, defend the method and limitation statement.

units.title: FISH, microarray and copy-number interpretation
objectives: Compare FISH, chromosomal microarray, SNP array and MLPA by analyte, resolution, scope and failure modes.
Apply the ACMG/ClinGen evidence-scoring framework to constitutional CNVs while separating classification from patient-specific causality.
Report uncertainty, inheritance, penetrance and evidence limitations clearly.
topics: Probe design: dual-fusion, break-apart, enumeration; metaphase/interphase
aCGH/SNP-array, copy-number, AOH/ROH/UPD, exon-focused CNV, MLPA
CNV dosage sensitivity, phenotype overlap, evidence scoring and reporting
units.casePractice: Use the open ClinGen dosage-sensitivity and CNV interpretation curation interfaces. Reuse only permitted public assertions and cite them; no downloaded patient-facing images.
units.assessment: Complete a mock evidence grid on a public ClinGen assertion, including alternative explanations and limitations.

units.title: Sequence testing technologies and analytic performance
objectives: Compare Sanger, PCR, targeted NGS, exome, genome, RNA, methylation and long-read approaches at the level of reportable variation.
Interpret sensitivity, specificity, analytic limits and coverage metrics in relation to assay validation.
Design a test-selection rationale for a fictional referral that identifies what a negative result does not exclude.
topics: DNA/RNA extraction, PCR variants, allele discrimination, sequencing chemistry, alignment/calling
Germline versus somatic NGS; CNV/SV, repeat and low-level mosaic detection
Preanalytic, analytic and postanalytic error; validation, verification and QC
units.casePractice: Review NIST/Genome in a Bottle benchmark concepts to assess assay performance; benchmark genomes are reference materials, not patient cases.
units.assessment: Write a one-page analytical validation outline with positive/negative controls, reportable range and limitations.

units.title: Variant interpretation and evidence calibration
objectives: Classify a Mendelian sequence variant using ACMG/AMP criteria and current ClinGen refinements.
Distinguish variant pathogenicity classification from causality in an individual and from clinical actionability.
Document evidence strength, conflict, transcript/genome assembly and date/version transparently.
topics: Five-tier terminology and evidence hierarchy; population, segregation, de novo, functional, computational data
ClinGen VCEP specifications; gene-disease validity; ClinVar review status/conflicts
VUS management and reclassification; splice/noncoding variants and limitations
units.casePractice: Use ClinVar/ClinGen public curation records to compare evidence and review status; do not infer clinical action from an isolated entry.
units.assessment: Submit a criterion-by-criterion mock classification with two uncertainties and one dissenting interpretation.

units.title: Constitutional genomic testing in clinical contexts
objectives: Choose and interpret testing for a fictional constitutional referral while respecting phenotype and inheritance limits.
Compare diagnostic, predictive, carrier, screening and prenatal testing purposes and consent requirements.
Explain residual risk and follow-up choices without turning a laboratory report into individual medical advice.
topics: Symptomatic diagnostic work-up; phenotype specificity; genotype-phenotype correlation
Predictive/carrier/reproductive screening, prenatal cfDNA and diagnostic confirmation
Residual risk, recurrence risk, incidental/secondary findings, informed consent
units.casePractice: Use published public ClinVar/ClinGen records as evidence examples; no identifiable registry narratives, patient records or images reproduced.
units.assessment: Create a concise test-selection and limitations note for three explicitly fictional vignettes.

units.title: Molecular mechanisms, imprinting, repeat expansion and epigenomics
objectives: Relate SNVs/indels, repeats, methylation/imprinting, mitochondrial heteroplasmy, LOH/AOH and NMD to suitable assays.
Explain why a technically negative test can fail to exclude a mechanism outside the validated assay scope.
Interpret methylation or episignature findings as assay/context-dependent evidence.
topics: Imprinting and methylation; X-inactivation; triplet repeat expansions
Mitochondrial variants/heteroplasmy, repeat instability and chromosomal instability
Nonsense-mediated decay, RNA studies and episignatures
units.casePractice: Use published ClinGen gene/variant summaries for mechanistic evidence; these are curation records, not raw cases.
units.assessment: Map five mechanisms to assays and identify an explicit blind spot for each.

units.title: Cancer cytogenomics and somatic molecular diagnostics
objectives: Distinguish constitutional findings from acquired clonal findings and interpret the clinical context of somatic results.
Apply current somatic variant classification concepts and separate oncogenicity from therapeutic evidence.
Integrate karyotype, FISH, copy-number and NGS observations without assuming interchangeable sensitivity.
topics: Clonal evolution, stemline/sideline, mainline, MRD monitoring and sample context
Somatic NGS, tumor purity, allele fraction, assay limits, structural alterations
AMP/ASCO/CAP tiers, CIViC evidence, evidence date and context-specific reporting
units.casePractice: Analyze public CIViC evidence records. They are interpreted database entries; clinical action depends on tumor, indication, current guidance and jurisdiction.
units.assessment: Write a mock somatic report interpretation paragraph that separates classification, evidence level and limitations.

units.title: Cytogenomic and molecular nomenclature
objectives: Translate constitutional and acquired findings into standardized report nomenclature within the learner’s competence.
Recognize that ISCN is a licensed standard and the 2026 ABMGG blueprint specifies ISCN 2024.
Avoid implying a single nomenclature describes method limitations or clinical significance.
topics: Constitutional numerical/structural/mosaic findings
Acquired clonal findings, cell counts and FISH patterns
CMA copy-number, AOH/ROH/UPD and sequence HGVS descriptors
units.casePractice: Use only openly described published examples; do not reproduce copyrighted ISCN tables or patient reports.
units.assessment: Correct five intentionally flawed fictional descriptions using source and nomenclature-version notes.

units.title: Laboratory management, quality and regulation
objectives: Design a quality-control and proficiency-testing response to a fictional failure signal.
Explain validation/verification, calibration, analytical performance and personnel competency.
Recognize CLIA/CAP/local regulatory scope without representing this course as laboratory authorization.
topics: Quality system, validation, QC, proficiency testing, competency, corrective action
Preanalytic/sample identity, contamination, chain-of-custody and safety
Regulatory frameworks; genetics-specific standards are frequently paywalled and must be obtained lawfully
units.casePractice: Use CDC/NIST public training materials and benchmark datasets; not patient records.
units.assessment: Complete a mock nonconformance report with root-cause analysis, corrective action and effectiveness check.

units.title: Ethics, consent, privacy and communication
objectives: Explain informed consent, assent, privacy and result communication at a principles level.
Distinguish HIPAA and GINA scope and state that neither eliminates all privacy or discrimination concerns.
Communicate uncertainty and limitations in plain language while directing clinical care questions to qualified clinicians.
topics: Genetic counseling boundaries; predictive and reproductive test consent
HIPAA/GINA overview, secondary findings, family implications and data sharing
Result reclassification, documentation, communicating VUS and no-result outcomes
units.casePractice: GenomeConnect is a patient registry/data-sharing resource, not a free-to-copy case library. Use its published materials only under their posted terms.
units.assessment: Draft a plain-language mock consent/limitation explanation for a fictional patient, then score with rubric.

units.title: Integrated diagnostic sign-out and board-style synthesis
objectives: Integrate method selection, analytic validity, variant evidence, nomenclature, QC and uncertainty in a simulated sign-out.
Prioritize board blueprint topics proportionally while identifying what lectures do not teach (hands-on competence and case volume).
Audit a report for internal consistency and provenance.
topics: End-to-end mock case workflow: requisition to report
Cross-domain integration and common interpretive traps
Exam blueprint synthesis and independent further study plan
units.casePractice: Construct a wholly fictional integrated case; use no real patient-level data and label every invented value as simulation.
units.assessment: Produce a mock report, oral defense and short reflection; no score predicts ABMGG exam outcomes.

assignment.title: Integrated laboratory interpretation portfolio
assignment.instructions: Use only the fictional scenarios included here or lawfully accessible public variant-curation resources. Do not copy patient images, reports or raw records. Submit: (1) a test-selection memo specifying indication, specimen and assay scope; (2) a mock variant/CNV evidence table with provenance and date; (3) a mock report including nomenclature, classification, uncertainty, limitations and follow-up questions; (4) an assay-quality/validation note; and (5) a 5-minute oral defense distinguishing variant classification, case-level causality and clinical actionability. Cite current primary resources. Do not provide patient-specific care.

rubric.performance: 20: method directly addresses question with validated limits; 10: partially justified; 0: method mismatch/unjustified.
25: criteria used with sources, strength, conflict and date; 12: incomplete provenance or over-weighting; 0: unsupported definitive label.
20: specimen, QC, reportable range and blind spots explicit; 10: material omission; 0: assumes universal detection.
15: internally consistent current-version notation and plain language; 8: minor errors; 0: materially misleading/unsupported.
10: no copied case material, terms respected, consent/privacy addressed; 0: rights/privacy violation.
10: separates classification/cause/actionability and states limits; 5: partial; 0: unwarranted clinical directive.

assignment.passingThreshold: No validated exam-passing threshold; suggested course completion threshold is 80/100 with no privacy/rights breach. This is not a board predictor.

assessment.formative: Unit retrieval exercises, self-checks and case debriefs; no clinical sign-out authority is conferred.
assessment.summative: 12 original board-cognitive questions plus the portfolio rubric. Question bank is educational, not official ABMGG content and not validated to predict board outcomes.

unitMap.text: Genome architecture, chromosomes and cell division
coveredTopics: Genome organization, chromatin packaging, centromeres/telomeres, nucleolar organizer regions
Mitosis/meiosis, gametogenesis, disjunction, recombination, mosaicism/chimerism
ISCN 2024 overview and limits of freely available nomenclature references

unitMap.text: Chromosomal disease mechanisms and constitutional cytogenetics
coveredTopics: Aneuploidy/polyploidy, structural rearrangements, balanced/unbalanced events, rings, markers, recombination
Constitutional karyotype, cell culture, banding, microscopy and specimen limitations
Mosaicism, maternal-cell contamination and prenatal specimen interpretation

unitMap.text: FISH, microarray and copy-number interpretation
coveredTopics: Probe design: dual-fusion, break-apart, enumeration; metaphase/interphase
aCGH/SNP-array, copy-number, AOH/ROH/UPD, exon-focused CNV, MLPA
CNV dosage sensitivity, phenotype overlap, evidence scoring and reporting

unitMap.text: Sequence testing technologies and analytic performance
coveredTopics: DNA/RNA extraction, PCR variants, allele discrimination, sequencing chemistry, alignment/calling
Germline versus somatic NGS; CNV/SV, repeat and low-level mosaic detection
Preanalytic, analytic and postanalytic error; validation, verification and QC

unitMap.text: Variant interpretation and evidence calibration
coveredTopics: Five-tier terminology and evidence hierarchy; population, segregation, de novo, functional, computational data
ClinGen VCEP specifications; gene-disease validity; ClinVar review status/conflicts
VUS management and reclassification; splice/noncoding variants and limitations

unitMap.text: Constitutional genomic testing in clinical contexts
coveredTopics: Symptomatic diagnostic work-up; phenotype specificity; genotype-phenotype correlation
Predictive/carrier/reproductive screening, prenatal cfDNA and diagnostic confirmation
Residual risk, recurrence risk, incidental/secondary findings, informed consent

unitMap.text: Molecular mechanisms, imprinting, repeat expansion and epigenomics
coveredTopics: Imprinting and methylation; X-inactivation; triplet repeat expansions
Mitochondrial variants/heteroplasmy, repeat instability and chromosomal instability
Nonsense-mediated decay, RNA studies and episignatures

unitMap.text: Cancer cytogenomics and somatic molecular diagnostics
coveredTopics: Clonal evolution, stemline/sideline, mainline, MRD monitoring and sample context
Somatic NGS, tumor purity, allele fraction, assay limits, structural alterations
AMP/ASCO/CAP tiers, CIViC evidence, evidence date and context-specific reporting

unitMap.text: Cytogenomic and molecular nomenclature
coveredTopics: Constitutional numerical/structural/mosaic findings
Acquired clonal findings, cell counts and FISH patterns
CMA copy-number, AOH/ROH/UPD and sequence HGVS descriptors

unitMap.text: Laboratory management, quality and regulation
coveredTopics: Quality system, validation, QC, proficiency testing, competency, corrective action
Preanalytic/sample identity, contamination, chain-of-custody and safety
Regulatory frameworks; genetics-specific standards are frequently paywalled and must be obtained lawfully

unitMap.text: Ethics, consent, privacy and communication
coveredTopics: Genetic counseling boundaries; predictive and reproductive test consent
HIPAA/GINA overview, secondary findings, family implications and data sharing

unitMap.text: Integrated diagnostic sign-out and board-style synthesis

topicGaps: The eight previously listed ESHG archive-linked YouTube candidates remain free/publicly advertised but their runtimes could not be observed: yt-dlp returned “Failed to extract any player response.” Their duration is null and all eight remain excluded from verified-hour totals.

Nine unique ARUP lecture pages were added with publisher-stated video lengths and public free-access statements. Their 8.1131 hours are the full observed external total in this packet; the remaining measured shortfall to 36 hours is 27.8869 hours. Scripts and clip-plan target minutes are not rendered or verified video.

Important residual instruction gaps include supervised cell culture, slide preparation and microscopy; hands-on FISH and assay operation; reportable-range validation for assay- and specimen-specific classes; proficiency testing and laboratory-specific QMS/regulatory application; detailed prenatal specimen interpretation; licensed ISCN practice; consent/privacy across jurisdictions; and sufficient case-based sign-out experience. Public lectures do not supply the accredited program’s case volume or all its didactics.

The four original episodes in the authored file are fully narrated source-based teaching scripts marked scripted; they are not rendered, uploaded, or counted. The existing 36-item originalClipPlan is preserved as planning material only; its targetMinutes are not media hours.

ACGME page lists the current LGG program requirements effective July 1, 2026; the public page identifies LGG separately under Medical Genetics and Genomics accreditation resources.

ABMGG exam requirements identify a laboratory specialty certification route for qualifying MD/DO/PhD trainees and separately state accredited laboratory postdoctoral training. It is neither a physician-only specialty nor the Clinical Genetics and Genomics residency track.

ABMGG blueprint effective August 2025 weights content as structure 10%, pathogenesis 20%, application/interpretation 53%, management 7% and nomenclature 10%. It notes ISCN 2024 for 2026 examinations. Re-check before future exam administrations.
The ABMGG board examination is real and distinct; this is not an additional ABMS-member board. Do not imply independent course completion makes a learner eligible.

Publicly viewable resources are not automatically licensed for republication. No patient images, reports, clinical record or identifiable data have been copied. Public variant databases contain curation records rather than a blanket grant to reuse underlying data.

topicGaps: The eight previously listed ESHG archive-linked YouTube candidates remain free/publicly advertised but their runtimes could not be observed: yt-dlp returned “Failed to extract any player response.” Their duration is null and all eight remain excluded from verified-hour totals.

Nine unique ARUP lecture pages were added with publisher-stated video lengths and public free-access statements. Their 8.1131 hours are the full observed external total in this packet; the remaining measured shortfall to 36 hours is 27.8869 hours. Scripts and clip-plan target minutes are not rendered or verified video.

Important residual instruction gaps include supervised cell culture, slide preparation and microscopy; hands-on FISH and assay operation; reportable-range validation for assay- and specimen-specific classes; proficiency testing and laboratory-specific QMS/regulatory application; detailed prenatal specimen interpretation; licensed ISCN practice; consent/privacy across jurisdictions; and sufficient case-based sign-out experience. Public lectures do not supply the accredited program’s case volume or all its didactics.

The four original episodes in the authored file are fully narrated source-based teaching scripts marked scripted; they are not rendered, uploaded, or counted. The existing 36-item originalClipPlan is preserved as planning material only; its targetMinutes are not media hours.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the Johns Hopkins programme and ABMGG pathway?

options.text: A physician-only two-year residency qualifying automatically for two ABMS boards.
A two-year ACGME-accredited LGG fellowship; ABMGG LGG certification is a laboratory specialty pathway open to qualifying MD/DO or PhD graduates after accredited laboratory training.
A research-only postdoctoral role with no separate examination.
A combined Pediatrics/Clinical Genetics residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins labels the JHH fellowship ACGME accredited and two years. ABMGG describes LGG as a laboratory specialty, accepts MD/DO/qualifying PhD, and requires ACGME-accredited laboratory postdoctoral training. It is neither physician-only nor the combined clinical genetics pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: A variant is classified as a VUS under an applicable Mendelian framework. Which inference is justified?

options.text: It is probably causal if the phenotype matches.
It should be used to direct irreversible predictive management.
Available evidence is insufficient or conflicting for a more definitive classification; classification alone does not establish patient-level causality.
It is benign unless confirmed by family testing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACMG/AMP framework has five categories; uncertain significance is not a proxy for pathogenicity or benignity, and variant classification must be distinguished from explaining a patient.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public ClinVar page has a pathogenic assertion with one-star review status and a conflicting benign assertion elsewhere. What is the best first step?

options.text: Accept the newest date and discard other evidence.
Examine submitting criteria, evidence, review status, transcript/build, conflicts and current expert-panel guidance before drawing a conclusion.
Average the two labels.
Treat all ClinVar assertions as expert-panel consensus.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public records differ in review status and evidence; expert curation and current evidence must be inspected, not inferred from a label.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which resource is most appropriate to begin structured interpretation of a constitutional copy-number variant?

practiceQuestions.rationale: Constitutional CNVs use the ACMG/ClinGen CNV evidence framework. Somatic tiers and sequence-missense predictions answer different questions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A negative exome is reported for a suspected disorder. Which statement is most defensible?

options.text: No genetic cause exists.
All structural and noncoding variation is excluded.
No reportable finding was detected within the assay’s validated design, analytic performance, specimen quality and interpretation scope; other mechanisms may remain.
The result rules out mosaicism in all tissues.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A test result must be bounded by analytic and postanalytic limitations. Exome assays do not universally detect all classes or mosaicism.

Select the assay that best matches the clinical question, suspected variant class, specimen and validated detection range.

practiceQuestions.stem: When interpreting mosaicism from culture-based cytogenetic analysis, what issue is especially important?

options.text: Any single abnormal cell proves constitutional mosaicism.
Cell counts, culture artifacts/pseudomosaicism, specimen source and orthogonal confirmation may affect interpretation.
Mosaicism and chimerism are synonyms.
Nomenclature alone establishes pathogenicity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The board blueprint covers mosaicism and pseudomosaicism; evidence must be interpreted in light of specimen and method. Nomenclature does not establish clinical significance.

options.text: Nomenclature is the majority domain.

rubric.evidence_and_sources: 30% — authoritative, current, accurately scoped sources; claims are traceable.
rubric.analytic_reasoning: 25% — assay fit, limitations, quality and data interpretation are explicit.
rubric.clinical_integration_and_uncertainty: 25% — phenotype/specimen context, differential, uncertainty and escalation are defensible.
rubric.communication_and_ethics: 20% — clear report, privacy, consent, equity and regulatory caveats.
rubric.passingStandard: Suggested educational threshold 80%; not validated, not a board score, and not permission for clinical work.

components: 10 original multiple-choice questions with source-linked rationales (no recalled/proprietary ABPath items).

Learner must pass unit tasks by self-check; no faculty calibration or human clinical review has been performed.
assessment.limitations: Assessments are not validated measures of clinical competence, board readiness or likelihood of passing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A family asks why an apparently pathogenic variant in a candidate gene does not yet establish a molecular diagnosis. Which statement best reflects gene–disease validity?

options.text: A candidate-gene variant can be classified pathogenic before the gene-disease relationship is established.
Variant classification alone cannot establish causality when the gene-disease association itself remains uncertain.
A rare variant is always pathogenic when phenotype is suggestive.
A ClinVar record is equivalent to an independent expert-panel assertion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A variant in a gene of uncertain significance cannot be called pathogenic for the proposed Mendelian disease solely from variant-level evidence; establish the gene-disease relationship first.

practiceQuestions.stem: A sequence variant is observed at low allele fraction in one specimen. Which next step is most defensible before reporting a constitutional germline call?

options.text: Assume constitutional heterozygosity and report without qualification.
Review specimen type, assay limit of detection, read-level evidence and possible mosaicism/contamination; select validated orthogonal follow-up if needed.
Convert the variant allele fraction directly to disease penetrance.
Exclude the finding because heterozygous variants must be near 50%.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Allele fraction is shaped by biology and assay factors. Check QC and specimen context, then use an appropriate validated confirmation; do not equate allele fraction with penetrance.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a genomic assay, coverage is poor across a repetitive region. A negative callset is requested to exclude a suspected disorder. What is the key reporting caution?

options.text: A negative sequencing result excludes all variant classes in the gene.
State relevant low-coverage/method limitations and whether another method may be needed; a negative result does not eliminate all genetic causes.
Replace the result with a VUS.
Infer the missing genotype from phenotype.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A negative result is bounded by assay design and performance. Explicitly describe the regions/classes not reliably assessed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Two ClinVar submissions disagree for a variant. Which action best supports a laboratory interpretation?

options.text: Use the majority vote across all submissions without checking evidence.
Review assertion criteria, review status, condition, submitter evidence and date, then apply current lab classification procedures.
Average the five-tier classifications.
Choose whichever classification appears first in the search results.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ClinVar aggregates submissions from different sources, and NIH states submissions are not independently verified; assess evidence, assertion criteria and context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 2015 ACMG/AMP classification framework is used for a variant in a gene with a disease-specific ClinGen expert-panel specification. What is the best practice?

options.text: Ignore all disease-specific specifications.
Check and apply current gene/disease-specific expert specifications where applicable, documenting the evidence and framework version.
Treat every criterion as equally strong.
Treat a VUS as actionable.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The general ACMG/AMP framework can be refined by ClinGen expert specifications. Criteria are evidence-weighted, and uncertainty should remain explicit.

practiceQuestions.stem: A tumor sequencing panel detects a drug-associated alteration. Which conclusion is justified from molecular result alone?

options.text: The drug is necessarily indicated for this patient.
The finding must be interpreted in the tumor type, assay, current product labeling/guidelines, clinical context and limitations; molecular detection alone does not establish treatment choice.
The same variant predicts response equally across cancers.
No other biomarker is needed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A biomarker result is not itself a prescription. FDA labeling varies, and not every biomarker entry specifies action; multidisciplinary interpretation is required.

practiceQuestions.stem: A targeted infectious NAAT is positive in a specimen from a nonsterile site. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Positive NAAT proves viable invasive infection.
Interpret detection alongside specimen site, clinical syndrome, pretest probability and assay limitations; nucleic-acid detection may not establish organism viability or causation.
Report disease severity from Ct alone.
Repeat testing until negative and disregard the first result.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Molecular detection must be interpreted in context. Multiplex/broad testing increases risk of incidental detection, colonization, and uncertain causality.

practiceQuestions.stem: A new laboratory-developed molecular assay is introduced. Which is the soundest initial quality approach?

options.text: Use published sensitivity claims without local performance studies.
Define intended use and applicable regulatory requirements, verify/validate performance characteristics and establish QC, procedures, competency and ongoing monitoring before patient use.
Validate only after a failed patient result.
Use a research benchmark sample as the sole evidence of clinical validity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical lab testing requires a quality system and method-specific performance assessment; reference benchmarks support analytic evaluation but do not substitute for clinical validation or regulatory compliance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A variant allele occurs at a frequency incompatible with a highly penetrant rare dominant disorder in the relevant ancestry, but an internet predictor calls it damaging. What is best?

options.text: Call it pathogenic because one computational tool is damaging.
Integrate ancestry-aware population frequency, phenotype, segregation, functional and other evidence under defined criteria; avoid using one tool alone.
Ignore population data.
Use the laboratory’s most frequent classification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Variant classification requires evidence types integrated under a documented framework; population data and computational predictions are not individually dispositive.

practiceQuestions.stem: NGS benchmark calls are used to compare two pipelines. Which limitation must be remembered?

options.text: Benchmark high-confidence regions guarantee equivalent sensitivity across every genome region and clinical assay.
Benchmark results are bounded by reference sample, region, variant type, platform and benchmark truth set; clinical assay validation remains separate.
NIST reference samples are patient cases.
A benchmark VCF establishes clinical utility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: GIAB provides carefully characterized benchmarking resources but they do not represent every difficult region or clinical use; benchmark performance is not clinical validation.

Describe how artifact, device material and treatment effects can mimic or obscure disease.
topics: Lens architecture and cataract; angle/trabecular meshwork; glaucoma-associated tissue change; intraocular lens/device-associated pathology; specimen context.
sourceUrls: Broad overview spanning orbit, retina, cornea, and cataract pathology.
IOL history, design, complications and pathology-relevant context.
Lens embryology, normal histopathology, and lens pathology.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional post-procedure specimen summary to list device, surgery and timing questions before interpretation.
units.assessment: Artifact-versus-lesion exercise and structured handoff.

units.title: Ocular and orbital tumors, including pediatric differentials
objectives: Build a compartment- and age-aware differential for intraocular/orbital mass and leukocoria; do not infer diagnosis from a single clinical sign.
State the role and limits of morphology and ancillary testing in tumor classification.
topics: Retinoblastoma, melanocytic lesions, metastases, vascular/mesenchymal and epithelial lesions; leukocoria differential; consultation and sampling limits.
boardDomains: Ocular and orbital neoplasia; pediatric eye disease and differential diagnosis.
sourceUrls: Vitreoretinal conditions including detachment, injury, vascular and diabetic patterns, radiation and leukemic retinopathy, and retinopathy of prematurity.
Retinoblastoma/leukocoria differential, iris and choroidal lesions, and ocular metastasis.
Pediatric anterior segment pathology and congenital/inflammatory differentials.
units.casePractice: Compare linked retinoblastoma teaching material with a fictional leukocoria differential; state why the fictional case is not a diagnosis.
units.assessment: Two-step differential: localize/describe first, then choose next information needed.

units.title: Optic nerve, orbit, lacrimal gland, and lymphoproliferative disease
objectives: Localize an orbital lesion to relevant anatomic compartments and distinguish optic-nerve, glandular, inflammatory and lymphoid categories.
Identify when systemic history, immunophenotyping, imaging or another service's expertise is needed.
topics: Optic-nerve and orbital histology; inflammatory and infectious disease; lymphoma; lacrimal gland lesions; imaging-to-pathology correlation.
sourceUrls: Broad overview spanning orbit, retina, cornea, and cataract pathology.
Neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory orbital conditions, including lacrimal/orbital differentials.
Gross/microscopic optic-nerve review, including congenital anomalies, drusen, edema, ischemia, and neoplasms.
Oculoplastic and adnexal topics including sebaceous carcinoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, lymphoma, lacrimal obstruction, and orbit.
units.casePractice: Describe one linked MGH optic-nerve/orbit slide and list appropriate clinical/laboratory correlation questions.
units.assessment: Differential tree with a defensible testing/consultation rationale.

units.title: Ancillary tests, molecular methods, and diagnostic uncertainty
objectives: Match special stains, immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence and molecular assays to a question rather than ordering/interpreting by rote.
Explain controls, specificity, tissue adequacy and why results must be reconciled with morphology and clinical context.
topics: Stains; immunophenotyping; molecular classification; digital/whole-slide review; quality, controls and interpretive limits.
boardDomains: Diagnostic methods, molecular pathology and quality; no independent certification domain inferred.
sourceUrls: Broad overview spanning orbit, retina, cornea, and cataract pathology.
units.casePractice: For a fictional tumor differential, choose one test, state the specific question, required control and an alternative explanation for a positive result.
units.assessment: Methods table graded on question-fit, controls, caveats and correlation.

units.title: Clinicopathologic synthesis, consultation, ethics, and final sign-out
objectives: Synthesize history, gross findings, histology and ancillary studies into a concise educational interpretation with explicit limitations.
Communicate uncertainty and request relevant correlation without claiming independent clinical authority or making unsupported management recommendations.
topics: Differential prioritization; second opinions; report clarity; privacy/rights; educational versus clinical interpretation; continuing review.
boardDomains: ACGME professionalism/communication and ophthalmic pathology disease-spectrum synthesis; no separate eye-pathology board exam.
sourceUrls: Broad overview spanning orbit, retina, cornea, and cataract pathology.
units.casePractice: Submit a fictional clinicopathologic case conference note using only licensed or linked images, then identify at least two unresolved alternatives.
units.assessment: Final portfolio rubric plus 10-item original knowledge check; explicitly formative, not board predictor.

assignment.title: Fictional clinicopathologic description and correlation portfolio
assignment.instructions: Choose three linked, source-authorized educational eye pathology slides (or use text-only case material). For each, state specimen/source provenance as provided, describe anatomy and morphology before naming a diagnosis, list a differential with evidence needed to distinguish it, note ancillary test rationale/limits, and write a brief educational report with uncertainty. Include citations and rights note. Do not copy patient images/records into the submission unless the source expressly licenses that exact use; link out instead. All constructed cases must be labelled fictional.

rubric.criterion: Accurate uncertainty, limitations and clinicopathologic correlation

assessment.format: Formative self-study: 10 original practice questions, module retrieval checks, three-case portfolio and rubric. No official board questions.
assessment.passingStandard: No validated or board-predictive passing cut score is claimed. Learner should review errors and discuss clinical interpretations only with qualified supervisors.
assessment.rubrics: Portfolio rubric above; each question has correct answer and explanatory rationale.
assessment.safety: No human clinical review performed; do not use for patient diagnosis, treatment, sign-out, specimen handling or credentialing.

studyHours.interpretation: Transparent self-study plan, not Hopkins curriculum, clinical training, or actual elapsed study time. The future-video portion is a production target only; current recorded readiness remains 7.77 unique observed hours and is 28.23 h short of the 36-hour video floor.

unitMap.text: Scope, specimen provenance, and diagnostic question
coveredTopics: Role boundaries; accessioning; clinical history; gross-to-slide workflow; communication and urgent-result escalation principles.

unitMap.text: Ocular and orbital anatomy, embryology, and normal histology
coveredTopics: Globe orientation, eyelid/adnexa, cornea, uvea, retina, optic nerve, orbit; normal tissue and layer-based localization.

unitMap.text: Specimen handling, gross examination, and reporting
coveredTopics: Globe/specimen receipt; orientation; fixation and processing concepts; sampling; gross description; microscopic description; synoptic clarity; communication.

unitMap.text: Eyelid, lacrimal drainage, and periocular adnexa
coveredTopics: Normal adnexal histology; cysts; squamous/basal-cell and sebaceous lesions; melanocytic lesions; lymphoma; margins and sampling limitations.

unitMap.text: Conjunctiva, cornea, and sclera
coveredTopics: Conjunctival epithelial lesions; melanocytic and lymphoid disease; corneal dystrophy/degeneration, infection and inflammation; scleral processes; tissue artifacts.

unitMap.text: Uvea, iris, ciliary body, and choroid
coveredTopics: Uveal anatomy; nevus/melanoma; inflammation; metastasis; specimen and biopsy limitations; prognostic markers as context-specific, not determinative alone.

unitMap.text: Retina, vitreous, and retinal pigment epithelium
coveredTopics: Layered retinal histology; ischemic/vascular injury; degeneration; retinoblastoma differential context; vitreous inflammation and metastasis.

unitMap.text: Lens, glaucoma, surgical devices, and treatment-related change
coveredTopics: Lens architecture and cataract; angle/trabecular meshwork; glaucoma-associated tissue change; intraocular lens/device-associated pathology; specimen context.

unitMap.text: Ocular and orbital tumors, including pediatric differentials
coveredTopics: Retinoblastoma, melanocytic lesions, metastases, vascular/mesenchymal and epithelial lesions; leukocoria differential; consultation and sampling limits.

unitMap.text: Optic nerve, orbit, lacrimal gland, and lymphoproliferative disease
coveredTopics: Optic-nerve and orbital histology; inflammatory and infectious disease; lymphoma; lacrimal gland lesions; imaging-to-pathology correlation.

unitMap.text: Ancillary tests, molecular methods, and diagnostic uncertainty
coveredTopics: Stains; immunophenotyping; molecular classification; digital/whole-slide review; quality, controls and interpretive limits.

unitMap.text: Clinicopathologic synthesis, consultation, ethics, and final sign-out
coveredTopics: Differential prioritization; second opinions; report clarity; privacy/rights; educational versus clinical interpretation; continuing review.

topicGaps: No separate official ophthalmic-pathology board exam or independent blueprint is listed in the cited current ABMS/ABPath sources; parent ophthalmology/pathology competencies remain an educational map, not a specialty examination blueprint.

Specimen accessioning, orientation, gross examination, sampling limits, report construction, and consultation workflow still lack long-form public video coverage; institutional supervised practice is not reproducible in self-study.
Anatomy, embryology, normal histology, and laboratory workflow have improved overview coverage but lack a coherent long-form integrated teaching sequence with specimen-to-report demonstrations.
Ocular-surface videos are more numerous, but scleral pathology, conjunctival lymphoid disease, infection-versus-degeneration distinctions, and tissue artifact interpretation remain unevenly covered.

Ancillary methods (special stains, immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, molecular testing, assay controls, validation, and uncertainty) lack sufficient dedicated, observed long-form video instruction.

Rare orbital, optic-nerve, lacrimal and lymphoid lesions; pediatric intraocular differentials; metastases; and modern clinicopathologic classification need deeper case-based instruction than the public lecture set provides.
Image repositories and videos remain link-only unless the specific source grants a matching reuse license; case access is not permission to copy, rehost, or use in clinical diagnosis.
Six original teaching episodes are scripted but not clinician-reviewed, rendered, or uploaded; the residual 19.78 verified-hour gap remains real.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One Johns Hopkins institutional offering, represented by two official pages with distinct exact display names (directory and Wilmer programme). The packet's generic physician-fellowship category is supported by Wilmer's completed-medical-school and USMLE requirements. The research component is supplementary to a clinical educational fellowship, not a separate non-physician/research-only fellowship. The directory explicitly says Non-Standard; no separate ACGME-accredited ophthalmic-pathology fellowship or combined board pathway was verified. Not a directory-only specialty invented from a category.
sourceCaveats: No saved prior MED-132 program/evidence files or saved research directory were present in the assigned paths at task start; research was resumed from primary source URLs rather than claiming to reuse nonexistent notes.
Hopkins's two public pages use different exact names for one institutional offering. Directory status is “Non-Standard”; no ACGME accreditation is inferred.

The research/clinical label and encouraged research activity are not a separate research-only/non-physician program. USMLE/medical-school statements appear on the official Wilmer page; individual eligibility must be checked with Hopkins.

ABMS/ABPath public lists do not show a distinct ophthalmic-pathology board or exam; ABO ophthalmology certification is a different primary specialty pathway. This is a current-list finding, not a claim about every society certificate.
ACGME ophthalmology requirements describe ophthalmic pathology study for ophthalmology residents; they are not accreditation of this fellowship or independent course.

No human clinical review has been performed. Materials need qualified clinical review before any institutional use; they do not confer affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, certification, procedure competence or guaranteed passing.
